item.title: Bayesian Regression: Does the Economy Decide American Elections?
item.description: Bayesian linear regression in R on 16 presidential elections: prior, likelihood and posterior on a grid, the closed-form posterior by hand, a Metropolis sampler by hand, the same answer from rstanarm, R-hat by hand, what the posterior lets you say and what it does not, forecasts with all the uncertainty, posterior predictive checks, leave-one-out by hand and with loo, errors with fat tails by changing the likelihood, how much the prior matters with sixteen rows, why Bayes factors depend on it even more, what calibrated means, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Bayesian linear regression in R on 16 presidential elections: prior, likelihood and posterior on a grid, the closed-form posterior by hand, a Metropolis sampler by hand, the same answer from rstanarm, R-hat by hand, what the posterior lets you say and what it does not, forecasts with all the uncertainty, posterior predictive checks, leave-one-out by hand and with loo, errors with fat tails by changing the likelihood, how much the prior matters with sixteen rows, why Bayes factors depend on it even more, what calibrated means, and APA reporting.

The question: sixteen elections

When the economy grows, the party in the White House is said to win the next election. Douglas Hibbs (2000) made a model of it, “bread and peace”: the growth of personal income during the term predicts the vote. How strong is the connection, and what does it say about an election in which growth is 2%?

There is a difficulty: there have been few elections. With 16 rows an ordinary regression gives a line and a wide interval, and nothing else. A Bayesian regression does two things more.

  • It starts with a prior: a distribution that says what we consider possible before we see the data. (A growth of 1% does not move the vote by 40 points.) The data then change the prior into the posterior.
  • Its answers are probabilities of the things we want to know: the probability that the slope is above 2, or that the party keeps the White House. An ordinary confidence interval does not say that, although everybody reads it that way.

The price is that one has to state the prior, and to say what happens with another. This page writes everything by hand, and gets the same numbers from the package rstanarm.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(rstanarm)    # stan_glm(): Bayesian regression with Stan behind it
# also used, with package::function: loo (loo, loo_compare), posterior (rhat, ess_bulk)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
# a probability from draws is never exactly 1
ptop <- function(p) if (p > 0.999) "over 99.9%" else pct(p, 1)
# APA: no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))

1. The data

Code 
hibbs <- read.table(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/avehtari/ROS-Examples/master/ElectionsEconomy/data/hibbs.dat",
  header = TRUE
)
names(hibbs)[1:5] <- c("year", "growth", "vote", "incumbent", "challenger")
hibbs
   year growth  vote  incumbent challenger
1  1952   2.40 44.60  Stevenson Eisenhower
2  1956   2.89 57.76 Eisenhower  Stevenson
3  1960   0.85 49.91      Nixon    Kennedy
4  1964   4.21 61.34    Johnson  Goldwater
5  1968   3.02 49.60   Humphrey      Nixon
6  1972   3.62 61.79      Nixon   McGovern
7  1976   1.08 48.95       Ford     Carter
8  1980  -0.39 44.70     Carter     Reagan
9  1984   3.86 59.17     Reagan    Mondale
10 1988   2.27 53.94  Bush, Sr.    Dukakis
11 1992   0.38 46.55  Bush, Sr.    Clinton
12 1996   1.04 54.74    Clinton       Dole
13 2000   2.36 50.27       Gore  Bush, Jr.
14 2004   1.72 51.24  Bush, Jr.      Kerry
15 2008   0.10 46.32     McCain      Obama
16 2012   0.95 52.00      Obama     Romney
Code 
y <- hibbs$vote
# centred growth: the intercept is then the vote at average growth
xc <- hibbs$growth - mean(hibbs$growth)
n <- length(y)

The 16 presidential elections from 1952 to 2012, from the book of Gelman et al. (2020), who updated the data of Hibbs (2000). vote is the share of the candidate of the incumbent party among the votes for the two large parties (%). growth is the growth of real personal income per head during the term (% per year), with more weight for the last quarters.

2. Look at the data

Code 
ls_fit <- lm(vote ~ growth, hibbs)
ggplot(hibbs, aes(growth, vote)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#eb6834") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = year), hjust = -0.2, vjust = 0.4, size = 3.4) +
  xlim(-0.6, 4.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Vote share of the party in the White House against growth",
    subtitle = "Orange: least squares",
    x = "growth of income during the term (% per year)",
    y = "vote (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
summary(ls_fit)$coefficients; c(sigma = sigma(ls_fit), confint(ls_fit)["growth", ])
             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 46.247648  1.6219314 28.513936 8.405474e-14
growth       3.060528  0.6962738  4.395581 6.099804e-04
   sigma    2.5 %   97.5 % 
3.763288 1.567169 4.553887

Each percentage point of growth goes with 3.1 points more of the vote, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.6 to 4.6. The points that lie far from the line are 1952 and 1968, the elections during the wars in Korea and Vietnam (“bread and peace”).

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: Bayes’ rule

\[\underbrace{p(\theta \mid y)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(y \mid \theta)}_{\text{likelihood}} \times \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}}, \qquad y_i \sim N(\alpha + \beta\,(x_i - \bar x),\ \sigma^2)\]

The likelihood says how well values of the parameters explain the data. Multiplied with the prior, it gives the probability of the values after seeing the data. The sign \(\propto\) means “up to a constant that makes the total 1”.

Step 2: one parameter on a grid

To see how it works, pretend that \(\alpha\) and \(\sigma\) are known (the values of least squares), so that only the slope \(\beta\) is unknown. Take a prior that is sceptical: a normal distribution around 0 with SD 1. Compute the three curves at many values of \(\beta\):

Code 
beta_grid <- seq(-3, 6, length.out = 400); a_hat <- mean(y); s_hat <- sigma(ls_fit)
prior_d <- dnorm(beta_grid, 0, 1)
lik <- exp(sapply(beta_grid, function(b) sum(dnorm(y, a_hat + b * xc, s_hat, log = TRUE))))
lik <- lik / sum(lik) / diff(beta_grid[1:2])
post_d  <- prior_d * lik; post_d <- post_d / sum(post_d) / diff(beta_grid[1:2])
gd <- data.frame(
  beta = rep(beta_grid, 3),
  density = c(prior_d, lik, post_d),
  curve = factor(
    rep(c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior"), each = 400),
    levels = c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior")
  )
)
ggplot(gd, aes(beta, density, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eda100", "#1baf7a", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "A sceptical prior, the data, and the result",
    x = "slope: points of the vote per 1% of growth",
    y = "density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
prec <- c(prior = 1, data = sum(xc^2) / s_hat^2)
c(
  mean_of_the_posterior_on_the_grid = sum(beta_grid * post_d) * diff(beta_grid[1:2]),
  precision_weighted_mean = sum(prec * c(0, coef(ls_fit)[["growth"]])) / sum(prec)
)
mean_of_the_posterior_on_the_grid           precision_weighted_mean 
                         2.061243                          2.061243

The posterior lies between the prior and the data. For normal distributions its mean is the mean of the two, weighted with their precision (1/variance):

\[E(\beta \mid y) = \frac{\text{prec}_{\text{prior}} \cdot \text{prior mean} + \text{prec}_{\text{data}} \cdot \hat\beta}{\text{prec}_{\text{prior}} + \text{prec}_{\text{data}}}\]

The data weigh 2.1 here, the prior 1. So this prior counts as much as 7.8 further elections would, next to the 16 that we have.

Step 3: the whole model in closed form

For the linear model there is a prior with which everything can be computed with a formula: the normal–inverse-gamma prior, \(\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(m_0, \sigma^2 V_0)\), \(\sigma^2 \sim IG(a_0, b_0)\). The posterior is of the same kind, with

\[V_n = (V_0^{-1} + X^\top X)^{-1}, \qquad m_n = V_n(V_0^{-1}m_0 + X^\top y),\]

\[a_n = a_0 + \tfrac n2, \qquad b_n = b_0 + \tfrac12\left(y^\top y + m_0^\top V_0^{-1}m_0 - m_n^\top V_n^{-1}m_n\right)\]

and each coefficient has a t distribution with \(2a_n\) degrees of freedom. With \(V_0^{-1} \to 0\), \(a_0 = -p/2\) and \(b_0 = 0\) (a flat prior) one gets the numbers of least squares:

Code 
nig <- function(X, y, m0, V0inv, a0, b0) {
  Vn <- solve(V0inv + crossprod(X))
  mn <- drop(Vn %*% (V0inv %*% m0 + crossprod(X, y)))
  an <- a0 + length(y) / 2
  bn <- b0 + (sum(y^2) + drop(t(m0) %*% V0inv %*% m0) - drop(t(mn) %*% solve(Vn, mn))) / 2
  data.frame(
    mean = mn,
    low = mn - qt(0.975, 2 * an) * sqrt(bn / an * diag(Vn)),
    high = mn + qt(0.975, 2 * an) * sqrt(bn / an * diag(Vn))
  )
}
X <- cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, growth = xc)
rbind(
  flat_prior_by_hand = nig(X, y, c(0, 0), diag(0, 2), -1, 0)["growth", ],
  least_squares = c(coef(ls_fit)["growth"], confint(ls_fit)["growth", ])
)
                       mean      low     high
flat_prior_by_hand 3.060528 1.567169 4.553887
least_squares      3.060528 1.567169 4.553887

With a flat prior the 95% credible interval is the 95% confidence interval. The numbers are the same, and what one may say about them is different.

Step 4: sampling

For most models there is no formula. Then one draws from the posterior. The oldest method (Metropolis et al., 1953) is a walk: propose a small random step; if the posterior is higher there, go; if it is lower, go with a probability equal to the ratio. The places visited are draws from the posterior, after a while. The constant in Bayes’ rule cancels in the ratio, so nobody needs to know it.

The priors (for the centred predictor):

  • \(\alpha \sim N(50, 5)\): with average growth the incumbent party gets about half of the votes, very probably between 40 and 60.
  • \(\beta \sim N(0, 5)\): 1% of growth changes the vote by less than 10 points, in an unknown direction. That is a weak statement, which is only to keep out absurd values.
  • \(\sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(1/5)\): elections deviate from the line by a few points, 5 on average.
Code 
log_posterior <- function(th, yy = y, xx = xc, prior_b = c(0, 5), t_errors = FALSE) {
  # th = (alpha, beta, log sigma)
  s <- exp(th[3])
  mu <- th[1] + th[2] * xx
  loglik <- if (t_errors) {
    sum(dt((yy - mu) / s, 4, log = TRUE) - log(s))
  } else {
    sum(dnorm(yy, mu, s, log = TRUE))
  }
  loglik +
    dnorm(th[1], 50, 5, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(th[2], prior_b[1], prior_b[2], log = TRUE) +
    dexp(s, 1 / 5, log = TRUE) +
    th[3] # + th[3]: because we walk on log sigma
}
metropolis <- function(draws, start, step, logp, ...) {
  out <- matrix(0, draws, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("alpha", "beta", "sigma")))
  now <- start
  lp <- logp(now, ...)
  for (i in seq_len(draws)) {
    candidate <- now + step * rnorm(3)
    lp_new <- logp(candidate, ...)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_new - lp) {
      now <- candidate
      lp <- lp_new
    }
    out[i, ] <- now
  }
  out[, 3] <- exp(out[, 3])
  out
}
set.seed(241); steps <- c(1.3, 1, 0.3); warm <- 2000; keep <- 20000
chains <- lapply(1:4, function(k) {
  metropolis(
    warm + keep,
    c(rnorm(1, 50, 8), rnorm(1, 0, 8), log(4) + rnorm(1)),
    steps,
    log_posterior
  )
})
hand <- do.call(rbind, lapply(chains, function(m) m[-(1:warm), ]))
summ <- function(v) {
  c(mean = mean(v), sd = sd(v), low = quantile(v, 0.025)[[1]], high = quantile(v, 0.975)[[1]])
}
t(apply(hand, 2, summ))
           mean        sd       low      high
alpha 51.966981 0.9900795 49.980349 53.913527
beta   2.993196 0.7523957  1.499903  4.464881
sigma  4.014293 0.8194796  2.770954  5.972682

Four chains, each from a different, deliberately bad start, and the first 2,000 steps of each thrown away (warm-up).

Code 
tr <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:4, function(k) {
    data.frame(i = 1:400, beta = chains[[k]][1:400, "beta"], chain = factor(k))
  })
)
ggplot(tr, aes(i, beta, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "The first 400 steps of four chains",
    subtitle = "They start in different places and meet",
    x = "step",
    y = "slope"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

Step 5: the same with a package

stan_glm() uses a much better sampler than ours (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) and the same model and priors. prior_intercept is for the centred predictor, like our \(\alpha\).

Code 
fit <- stan_glm(
  vote ~ growth,
  data = hibbs,
  prior = normal(0, 5),
  prior_intercept = normal(50, 5),
  prior_aux = exponential(1 / 5),
  seed = 242,
  refresh = 0,
  iter = 10000
)
stan <- as.matrix(fit) # columns: (Intercept) at growth 0, growth, sigma
stan_tab <- rbind(
  alpha = summ(stan[, "(Intercept)"] + stan[, "growth"] * mean(hibbs$growth)),
  beta = summ(stan[, "growth"]),
  sigma = summ(stan[, "sigma"])
)
round(cbind(hand = t(apply(hand, 2, summ)), stan = stan_tab), 2)
       mean   sd   low  high  mean   sd   low  high
alpha 51.97 0.99 49.98 53.91 51.97 1.00 49.97 53.95
beta   2.99 0.75  1.50  4.46  3.00 0.75  1.50  4.50
sigma  4.01 0.82  2.77  5.97  4.00 0.82  2.76  5.90
Code 
difference <- max(abs(t(apply(hand, 2, summ))[, c("mean", "sd")] - stan_tab[, c("mean", "sd")]))

(First four columns: our walk; last four: rstanarm.) They agree: the largest difference in a mean or SD is 0.02.

Did the chains arrive?

The check is the R-hat of Gelman and Rubin: the variance of all draws together, against the variance within each chain. If the chains are in different places the first is larger. By hand, with every chain cut in two halves, so that a drift within a chain also shows:

\[\hat R = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{m-1}{m}W + \frac 1m B}{W}}\]

(\(m\): length of a half; \(W\): mean of the variances within the halves; \(B\): \(m\) times the variance of the means of the halves. Values above 1.01 are suspicious; Vehtari et al., 2021, recommend a version based on ranks.)

Code 
halves <- function(cs) {
  do.call(
    cbind,
    lapply(cs, function(v) {
      m <- length(v) / 2
      cbind(v[1:m], v[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
    })
  )
}
rhat_hand <- function(cs) {
  h <- halves(cs)
  m <- nrow(h)
  W <- mean(apply(h, 2, var))
  B <- m * var(colMeans(h))
  sqrt(((m - 1) / m * W + B / m) / W)
}
get <- function(p) lapply(chains, function(m) m[-(1:warm), p])
diag_tab <- sapply(c("alpha", "beta", "sigma"), function(p) {
  c(
    R_hat_by_hand = rhat_hand(get(p)),
    R_hat_rank = posterior::rhat(do.call(cbind, get(p))),
    effective_draws = posterior::ess_bulk(do.call(cbind, get(p)))
  )
})
round(diag_tab, 4)
                    alpha      beta     sigma
R_hat_by_hand      1.0004    1.0005    1.0002
R_hat_rank         1.0004    1.0005    1.0002
effective_draws 6597.7163 6964.2780 7363.7930
Code 
rhat_first <- rhat_hand(lapply(chains, function(m) m[1:100, "beta"]))
c(R_hat_of_the_first_100_steps = rhat_first)
R_hat_of_the_first_100_steps 
                    2.307847
Code 
ess_stan <- posterior::ess_bulk(matrix(stan[, "growth"], ncol = 4))

R-hat is 1.00 for all. (With only the first 100 steps it is 2.31.) The effective number of draws tells how many independent draws the walk is worth: 6,964 out of 80,000 for the slope. rstanarm gets 16,141 out of 20,000.

4. Reading the output

Code 
print(fit, digits = 2)
stan_glm
 family:       gaussian [identity]
 formula:      vote ~ growth
 observations: 16
 predictors:   2
------
            Median MAD_SD
(Intercept) 46.30   1.67 
growth       3.00   0.71 
Auxiliary parameter(s):
      Median MAD_SD
sigma 3.88   0.74  
------
* For help interpreting the printed output see ?print.stanreg
* For info on the priors used see ?prior_summary.stanreg
Code 
posterior_interval(fit, prob = 0.95)
                 2.5%     97.5%
(Intercept) 42.794880 49.754346
growth       1.501168  4.499976
sigma        2.761800  5.904736
Code 
b <- hand[, "beta"]
c(P_slope_above_0 = mean(b > 0), P_slope_above_2 = mean(b > 2), P_slope_above_4 = mean(b > 4))
P_slope_above_0 P_slope_above_2 P_slope_above_4 
      0.9995875       0.9105875       0.0857000

The median is the middle of the posterior, the MAD_SD a robust SD. What we may say now:

  • The slope is probably between 1.5 and 4.5 (95% credible interval), with a mean of 3.0.
  • The probability that growth goes with more votes is over 99.9%. The probability that the slope is above 2 is 91%, above 4 9%.
  • Those are probabilities given the model and the prior. They say nothing about whether the line is a good model.

A forecast

In 2016 income was growing by about 2% (Gelman et al., 2020). The forecast for a new election uses all the uncertainty: for every draw of the parameters, draw a new vote.

\[p(y^* \mid y) = \int p(y^* \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta\]

Code 
set.seed(243)
line_2 <- hand[, "alpha"] + hand[, "beta"] * (2 - mean(hibbs$growth))
vote_2 <- line_2 + rnorm(nrow(hand), 0, hand[, "sigma"])
cbind(
  value = c(
    mean = mean(vote_2),
    low = quantile(vote_2, 0.025)[[1]],
    high = quantile(vote_2, 0.975)[[1]],
    P_incumbent_party_above_50 = mean(vote_2 > 50),
    P_line_above_50 = mean(line_2 > 50)
  )
)
                                value
mean                       52.2795996
low                        43.9318632
high                       60.6317892
P_incumbent_party_above_50  0.7153875
P_line_above_50             0.9863750
Code 
ggplot(
  rbind(
    data.frame(v = line_2, what = "where the line is"),
    data.frame(v = vote_2, what = "a new election")
  ),
  aes(v, fill = what)
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 51.1, colour = "#eb6834") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 55.5,
    y = 0.36,
    label = "result of 2016: 51.1",
    hjust = 0,
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(38, 66)) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast for an election with 2% growth",
    x = "vote of the party in the White House (%)",
    y = "density"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The expected vote is 52.3%. The line is above 50 at this growth with a probability of 99%, but a single election is much less certain: the probability of more than half is 72%. (The book gets 72%.) The result of 2016 was 51.1% for the candidate of the party in the White House, close to the middle of the distribution. (Hillary Clinton had more votes and lost the election. The model is about votes.)

5. Is the model any good?

Simulate the data that the model expects

If the model is right, data simulated from it should look like the real ones. For every tenth draw of the parameters make 16 new elections, and compare the largest deviation from the line:

Code 
pick <- seq(1, nrow(hand), by = 10); set.seed(244)
biggest <- function(v) max(abs(residuals(lm.fit(X, v))))
rep_stat <- apply(hand[pick, ], 1, function(p) biggest(p[1] + p[2] * xc + rnorm(n, 0, p[3])))
obs_stat <- biggest(y)
c(observed = obs_stat, P_simulated_at_least_as_large = mean(rep_stat >= obs_stat))
                     observed P_simulated_at_least_as_large 
                     8.992915                      0.259750
Code 
ggplot(data.frame(rep_stat), aes(rep_stat)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_stat, colour = "#eb6834", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Largest deviation from the line in simulated elections",
    subtitle = "Orange: in the real data",
    x = "points of the vote",
    y = "simulations"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

The real data have one election (1952) that is 9.0 points from the line. The model makes one at least as far in 26% of the simulations, so this alone is no reason to doubt the normal errors.

Leave one out

How well does the model predict an election that it has not seen? For every election, take it out, sample again, and compute the log density of the real result. Then the sum, called elpd. One can also get it without sampling again, from the draws (by reweighting them), which is what loo() does, in a refined version:

Code 
set.seed(245)
exact <- sapply(1:n, function(i) {
  d <- metropolis(7000, c(52, 3, log(4)), steps, log_posterior, yy = y[-i], xx = xc[-i])[
    -(1:1000),
  ]
  log(mean(dnorm(y[i], d[, 1] + d[, 2] * xc[i], d[, 3])))
})
weighted <- sapply(1:n, function(i) {
  -log(mean(1 / dnorm(y[i], hand[, 1] + hand[, 2] * xc[i], hand[, 3])))
})
loo_growth <- suppressWarnings(loo(fit))
fit0 <- stan_glm(
  vote ~ 1,
  data = hibbs,
  prior_intercept = normal(50, 5),
  prior_aux = exponential(1 / 5),
  seed = 246,
  refresh = 0,
  iter = 10000
)
loo_none <- suppressWarnings(loo(fit0))
c(
  exact_by_hand = sum(exact),
  reweighting_by_hand = sum(weighted),
  loo_package = loo_growth$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"],
  without_growth = loo_none$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"]
)
      exact_by_hand reweighting_by_hand         loo_package      without_growth 
          -46.37669           -46.14305           -46.30613           -51.59044
Code 
point_diff <- loo_growth$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - loo_none$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
elpd_diff <- sum(point_diff)
elpd_se <- sqrt(n) * sd(point_diff)
k_bad <- which(loo::pareto_k_values(loo_growth) > 0.7)
c(difference = elpd_diff, se = elpd_se); c(influential_elections = hibbs$year[k_bad])
difference         se 
  5.284311   3.899148 
influential_elections 
                 1952

The three ways of computing the elpd of the model with growth agree within 0.23. Growth improves the prediction by 5.3 (SE 3.9): more than its standard error, but less than two of them. With 16 elections, even a strong connection is hard to prove in new data. The package warns that the weights are unreliable for 1952, an election with a large influence (Vehtari et al., 2017). That is what the exact version is for.

Fat tails: change the likelihood

Two elections were decided by wars. A model that expects an outlier now and then has errors with a t distribution (4 degrees of freedom). In our sampler that is a switch:

Code 
set.seed(247)
robust <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:4, function(k) {
    metropolis(warm + keep, c(52, 3, log(3)), steps, log_posterior, t_errors = TRUE)[-(1:warm), ]
  })
)
rbind(`normal errors` = summ(hand[, "beta"]), `t errors, 4 df` = summ(robust[, "beta"]))
                   mean        sd      low     high
normal errors  2.993196 0.7523957 1.499903 4.464881
t errors, 4 df 3.273493 0.6106044 1.942135 4.389692

The slope is 3.27 instead of 2.99, and its SD is 0.61 instead of 0.75. The two elections of the wars do not make the result; they pull it down a little. (See robust regression.)

6. How much does the prior matter?

Six persons, six priors for the slope, the same sixteen elections:

Code 
priors <- list(
  `no opinion: N(0, 50)` = c(0, 50),
  `ours: N(0, 5)` = c(0, 5),
  `careful: N(0, 2)` = c(0, 2),
  `sceptic: N(0, 0.5)` = c(0, 0.5),
  `believer: N(4, 0.5)` = c(4, 0.5),
  `contrarian: N(-2, 0.5)` = c(-2, 0.5)
)
set.seed(248)
sens <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(priors), function(p) {
    d <- metropolis(22000, c(52, 1, log(4)), steps, log_posterior, prior_b = priors[[p]])[
      -(1:2000),
      "beta"
    ]
    data.frame(
      prior = p,
      prior_mean = priors[[p]][1],
      prior_sd = priors[[p]][2],
      mean = mean(d),
      low = quantile(d, 0.025)[[1]],
      high = quantile(d, 0.975)[[1]],
      P_above_0 = mean(d > 0)
    )
  })
)
print(data.frame(prior = sens$prior, round(sens[, 4:7], 2)), row.names = FALSE)
                  prior  mean   low  high P_above_0
   no opinion: N(0, 50)  3.05  1.52  4.62      1.00
          ours: N(0, 5)  2.97  1.47  4.44      1.00
       careful: N(0, 2)  2.71  1.26  4.05      1.00
     sceptic: N(0, 0.5)  0.70 -0.29  1.61      0.92
    believer: N(4, 0.5)  3.69  2.90  4.53      1.00
 contrarian: N(-2, 0.5) -1.34 -2.36 -0.34      0.00
Code 
sens$prior <- factor(sens$prior, levels = rev(sens$prior))
ggplot(sens, aes(y = prior)) +
  geom_linerange(
    aes(
      xmin = pmax(-4, prior_mean - 1.96 * prior_sd),
      xmax = pmin(7, prior_mean + 1.96 * prior_sd)
    ),
    colour = "#eda100",
    linewidth = 2.4,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean), colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(ls_fit)[["growth"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Prior (yellow) and posterior (blue) of the slope",
    subtitle = "95% ranges, cut at -4 and 7. Dashed: least squares",
    x = "points of the vote per 1% of growth",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
Code 
se_ <- function(p, w) sens[[w]][sens$prior == p]
  • With the three weak priors the result is nearly the same (mean between 2.7 and 3.0).
  • The strong opinions stay: the sceptic moves only to 0.7, the believer ends at 3.7 and the contrarian at -1.3. A prior with an SD of 0.5 counts as much as 31 elections, twice as many as there have been in the data.
  • So sixteen elections are not enough to convince a person with a strong opinion in the other direction.

So the prior is a part of the result, and it is reported. A prior that comes from outside (other countries, other elections) is knowledge. A prior that is made to get a result is a cheat, and it can be seen in this plot.

Bayes factors depend on it even more

A Bayes factor compares two hypotheses, here “the slope is 0” with “the slope is something, distributed like the prior”. It asks how well each predicted the data, so a very wide prior (a slope of 80 is possible) predicts badly. With flat priors for \(\alpha\) and \(\log\sigma\), the likelihood of the slope alone has a formula, \(L(\beta) \propto \left(S + S_{xx}(\beta - \hat\beta)^2\right)^{-(n-1)/2}\), and one integral does the rest:

Code 
S <- sum(residuals(ls_fit)^2); Sxx <- sum(xc^2); b_hat <- coef(ls_fit)[["growth"]]
L  <- function(b) (1 + Sxx * (b - b_hat)^2 / S)^(-(n - 1) / 2)
bf <- data.frame(prior_sd = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 20, 100, 1000))
bf$bayes_factor_for_an_effect <- sapply(bf$prior_sd, function(s) {
  integrate(function(b) L(b) * dnorm(b, 0, s), b_hat - 8, b_hat + 8, rel.tol = 1e-9)$value / L(0)
})
bf$posterior_mean <- sapply(bf$prior_sd, function(s) {
  den <- integrate(function(b) L(b) * dnorm(b, 0, s), b_hat - 8, b_hat + 8)$value
  integrate(function(b) b * L(b) * dnorm(b, 0, s), b_hat - 8, b_hat + 8)$value / den
})
print(round(bf, 2), row.names = FALSE)
 prior_sd bayes_factor_for_an_effect posterior_mean
    5e-01                       2.75           0.70
    1e+00                      19.04           1.90
    2e+00                      79.24           2.69
    5e+00                      77.91           2.99
    2e+01                      23.36           3.06
    1e+02                       4.73           3.06
    1e+03                       0.47           3.06

From an SD of 5 to one of 1,000 the posterior of the slope hardly changes (mean 2.99 and 3.06). The Bayes factor goes from 77.9 in favour of an effect to 0.47, which is against one. A default, very wide prior makes the “no effect” win in the end, whatever the data say (the Lindley paradox). Use Bayes factors only with priors that you would defend.

7. What “calibrated” means

A credible interval is right on average over the prior: if the true values really came from the prior, 95% of the 95% intervals contain them. It is not right for every single true value. We can check both, with the formula of step 3 (here with a narrow prior for the slope, \(\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(0, (\sigma/2)^2)\) and \(\sigma^2 \sim IG(5, 60)\)):

Code 
set.seed(249); V0inv <- diag(c(1 / 4, 4)); m0 <- c(50, 0); a0 <- 5; b0 <- 60
sim_once <- function(beta_fixed = NULL) {
  s2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, a0, b0)
  a <- rnorm(1, 50, sqrt(4 * s2))
  bt <- if (is.null(beta_fixed)) rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(s2 / 4)) else beta_fixed * sqrt(s2 / 4)
  r <- nig(X, a + bt * xc + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(s2)), m0, V0inv, a0, b0)["growth", ]
  r$low < bt && bt < r$high
}
cal <- c(
  `true slope drawn from the prior` = mean(replicate(3000, sim_once())),
  `true slope 1 prior SD from 0` = mean(replicate(3000, sim_once(1))),
  `true slope 3 prior SDs from 0` = mean(replicate(3000, sim_once(3)))
)
cbind(coverage = round(cal, 3))
                                coverage
true slope drawn from the prior    0.948
true slope 1 prior SD from 0       0.949
true slope 3 prior SDs from 0      0.897

Drawn from the prior: 94.8%. For a true slope that the prior considers very unlikely (3 SDs away) it is 89.7%. A frequentist confidence interval has its 95% for every value, and does not use any knowledge. Choose what you need, and say which.

8. Things to keep in mind

  • Write down the prior before you look, in units that a reader understands. Simulate from it (a prior predictive check) and see if it expects absurd data.
  • Centre the predictors: then the prior of the intercept is about the outcome at average values.
  • Report what the result looks like with other priors, at least a wider and a narrower one.
  • Check R-hat and the effective draws for every parameter, and look at the trace plots. rstanarm gives warnings about divergent transitions: do not ignore them.
  • The posterior is conditional on the model. Check it as you would any regression: simulated data, residuals, leave-one-out.
  • Probabilities of hypotheses (“99% that the slope is positive”) need the prior. Do not present them as a p value.
  • With many rows the prior hardly matters. With few, it does, and that is exactly when it helps.
  • Multilevel models are where Bayesian methods shine, because they estimate variances of small groups without trouble: stan_glmer() or brms::brm(). See multilevel models.
  • Relatives: the normal prior is ridge regression as a probability, and a prior on functions is a Gaussian process.

9. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the model with the distribution of the errors, every prior, the software with the number of chains and draws, the diagnostics, the posterior (mean or median, interval), checks of the model, and how the result changes with the prior (see the guidelines of Kruschke, 2021). The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
row_of <- function(label, m, se, lo, hi) {
  data.frame(
    Parameter = label,
    mean = f2(m),
    sd = f2(se),
    ci = paste0("[", f2(lo), ", ", f2(hi), "]")
  )
}
apa_table <- rbind(
  row_of(
    "Vote at average growth (%)",
    stan_tab["alpha", "mean"],
    stan_tab["alpha", "sd"],
    stan_tab["alpha", "low"],
    stan_tab["alpha", "high"]
  ),
  row_of(
    "Growth (points of the vote per 1%)",
    stan_tab["beta", "mean"],
    stan_tab["beta", "sd"],
    stan_tab["beta", "low"],
    stan_tab["beta", "high"]
  ),
  row_of(
    "Residual SD (points)",
    stan_tab["sigma", "mean"],
    stan_tab["sigma", "sd"],
    stan_tab["sigma", "low"],
    stan_tab["sigma", "high"]
  )
)
p_pos_stan <- mean(stan[, "growth"] > 0)
max_rhat <- max(apply(stan, 2, function(v) posterior::rhat(matrix(v, ncol = 4))))

Method (data analysis):

The vote share of the party holding the White House in the 16 presidential elections from 1952 to 2012 was regressed on the growth of real personal income per head during the term (Gelman et al., 2020; Hibbs, 2000), centred at its mean, with a Bayesian linear model with normal errors. The priors were N(50, 5) for the vote share at average growth, N(0, 5) for the slope (points per 1% of growth), and Exponential(1/5) for the residual standard deviation. The posterior was sampled with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (R package rstanarm; four chains of 10,000 iterations, half of them warm-up); convergence was judged with R-hat and the effective number of draws. We report posterior means, standard deviations and 95% credible intervals, the model was checked with posterior predictive simulations and leave-one-out cross-validation (Vehtari et al., 2017), and the sensitivity to the prior of the slope was examined with six priors and with t-distributed errors. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

All chains converged (R-hat ≤ 1.000; at least 16,100 effective draws for the slope). One percentage point of growth was associated with 3.0 points more of the vote (posterior SD = 0.75, 95% credible interval [1.5, 4.5]; posterior probability of a positive slope over 99.9%; Table 1). The residual standard deviation was 4.0 points. Growth improved the expected log predictive density by 5.3 (SE = 3.9). For a growth of 2% the predicted share was 52.3% (95% prediction interval [43.9, 60.6]), with a probability of 72% of exceeding one half. The posterior mean of the slope was between 2.7 and 3.0 for weak priors and between -1.3 and 3.7 for strong ones; with t-distributed errors it was 3.3.

Table 1

Posterior of the Regression of the Incumbent Party’s Vote on Economic Growth

Parameter Mean SD 95% credible interval
Vote at average growth (%) 51.97 1.00 [49.97, 53.95]
Growth (points of the vote per 1%) 3.00 0.75 [1.50, 4.50]
Residual SD (points) 4.00 0.82 [2.76, 5.90]

Note. N = 16 elections. Priors: see text.

Points to remember:

  • Give every prior and the reason for it.
  • Report R-hat and the effective draws.
  • Say “credible interval”, and say that probabilities are given the model and the prior.
  • Show what other priors would give.

10. Summary

When Few data, knowledge from outside, probabilities of the parameters and forecasts wanted, hierarchical models
The rule Posterior \(\propto\) likelihood × prior
Linear model Closed form (normal–inverse-gamma), or sampling
Sampling Metropolis (by hand), Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan)
How (R) stan_glm(y ~ x, prior = normal(0, 5), prior_intercept = normal(50, 5), prior_aux = exponential(0.2))
Read Mean or median, credible interval, probabilities, forecasts
Check R-hat, effective draws, simulated data, leave-one-out, other priors
Danger Strong priors with few data, Bayes factors with default priors
Related pages Simple regression, regularized regression, multilevel models, Gaussian processes

References

Gelman, A., Hill, J., & Vehtari, A. (2020). Regression and other stories. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781139161879

Hibbs, D. A. (2000). Bread and peace voting in U.S. presidential elections. Public Choice, 104(1–2), 149–180. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1005292312412

Kruschke, J. K. (2021). Bayesian analysis reporting guidelines. Nature Human Behaviour, 5(10), 1282–1291. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01177-7

Metropolis, N., Rosenbluth, A. W., Rosenbluth, M. N., Teller, A. H., & Teller, E. (1953). Equation of state calculations by fast computing machines. The Journal of Chemical Physics, 21(6), 1087–1092. https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., & Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing, 27(5), 1413–1432. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., Simpson, D., Carpenter, B., & Bürkner, P.-C. (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R̂ for assessing convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis, 16(2), 667–718. https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Difference-in-Differences: Does a Higher Minimum Wage Cost Jobs?
item.description: Difference-in-differences in R on the 410 fast-food restaurants of Card and Krueger: the four means, the same number from a regression, from changes and from two-way fixed effects, clustered standard errors by hand, the parallel trends assumption, comparisons within New Jersey, other outcomes and definitions, how small a difference in trends or a shock to a state changes the conclusion, why controlling for the first value gives another answer, what goes wrong when a treatment comes in waves (two-way fixed effects against group-time effects by hand and with did), and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Difference-in-differences in R on the 410 fast-food restaurants of Card and Krueger: the four means, the same number from a regression, from changes and from two-way fixed effects, clustered standard errors by hand, the parallel trends assumption, comparisons within New Jersey, other outcomes and definitions, how small a difference in trends or a shock to a state changes the conclusion, why controlling for the first value gives another answer, what goes wrong when a treatment comes in waves (two-way fixed effects against group-time effects by hand and with did), and APA reporting.

The question: two states and a law

On 1 April 1992 the minimum wage in New Jersey rose from $4.25 to $5.05 an hour. In Pennsylvania, on the other side of the river, it stayed at $4.25. What happened to the jobs in fast-food restaurants, where many people earn the minimum?

Two simple comparisons come to mind, and both are wrong:

  • New Jersey after against before. But 1992 was a year of recession. Jobs may have changed anyway.
  • New Jersey against Pennsylvania, after. But the restaurants in the two states may have been different from the start.

Difference-in-differences (DiD) combines them. The change in Pennsylvania shows what happened anyway. The change in New Jersey, minus the change in Pennsylvania, is the effect of the law. It is simple enough for a pocket calculator. What it needs is one assumption, and most of this page is about that one.

The study by Card and Krueger (1993, published in the American Economic Review in 1994) is one of the best-known in economics, and one of the most disputed. This page uses it to teach the method. It does not settle the question.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(fixest)      # feols(): regression with fixed effects and clustered errors
# also used, with package::function: did (att_gt, aggte), quantreg (rq)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
pval <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
}
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

1. The data

Code 
zip_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file(
  "https://davidcard.berkeley.edu/data_sets/njmin.zip",
  zip_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
data_file <- unzip(zip_file, "public.dat", exdir = tempfile("njmin"))
names_in_codebook <- c(
  "sheet", "chain", "co_owned", "state", "southj", "centralj", "northj", "pa1", "pa2", "shore",
  "ncalls", "empft", "emppt", "nmgrs", "wage_st", "inctime", "firstinc", "bonus", "pctaff", "meals",
  "open", "hrsopen", "psoda", "pfry", "pentree", "nregs", "nregs11", "type2", "status2", "date2",
  "ncalls2", "empft2", "emppt2", "nmgrs2", "wage_st2", "inctime2", "firstin2", "special2", "meals2",
  "open2r", "hrsopen2", "psoda2", "pfry2", "pentree2", "nregs2", "nregs112"
)
stores <- read.table(data_file, col.names = names_in_codebook, na.strings = ".")
stores$id <- seq_len(nrow(stores)) # (one sheet number is used twice)
stores$nj <- stores$state # 1 New Jersey, 0 Pennsylvania
# full-time equivalents, first interview
stores$fte1 <- stores$empft + stores$nmgrs + 0.5 * stores$emppt
stores$fte2 <- stores$empft2 + stores$nmgrs2 + 0.5 * stores$emppt2 # second interview
table(
  state = ifelse(stores$nj == 1, "New Jersey", "Pennsylvania"),
  second_interview = stores$status2
)
              second_interview
state            0   1   2   3   4   5
  New Jersey     1 321   2   5   1   1
  Pennsylvania   0  78   0   1   0   0

Card and Krueger interviewed 410 restaurants of four chains (Burger King, KFC, Roy Rogers, Wendy’s), 331 in New Jersey and 79 in eastern Pennsylvania. The first interview was in February and March 1992, before the law, the second in November and December. The outcome is employment in full-time equivalents (FTE): full-time employees and managers count 1, part-time employees a half. The six restaurants that had closed for good (status 3) have an employment of zero in the second interview. The file is on David Card’s web page.

2. Look at the data

Did the law do anything to the wages? The starting wage in both interviews:

Code 
w <- rbind(
  data.frame(state = stores$nj, wage = stores$wage_st, wave = "before"),
  data.frame(state = stores$nj, wage = stores$wage_st2, wave = "after")
)
w$state <- ifelse(w$state == 1, "New Jersey", "Pennsylvania")
w$wave <- factor(w$wave, levels = c("before", "after"))
w <- subset(w, !is.na(wage))
w$share <- ave(w$wage, w$state, w$wave, FUN = function(v) 1 / length(v))
ggplot(w, aes(wage, weight = share, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(4.2, 5.8, by = 0.1), colour = "white") +
  facet_grid(state ~ wave) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Starting wages before and after the law",
    x = "starting wage (dollars per hour)",
    y = "share of restaurants"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
wage_means <- with(
  stores,
  rbind(
    `New Jersey` = c(
      before = mean(wage_st[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
      after = mean(wage_st2[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    Pennsylvania = c(mean(wage_st[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE), mean(wage_st2[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)
round(wage_means, 2)
             before after
New Jersey     4.61  5.08
Pennsylvania   4.63  4.62
Code 
at_min <- mean(abs(stores$wage_st2[stores$nj == 1] - 5.05) < 0.001, na.rm = TRUE)

It did. Before, the two states looked the same. After, 89% of the restaurants in New Jersey paid exactly the new minimum, and nothing had changed in Pennsylvania. The mean starting wage rose by 0.47 dollars, or 10%.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: four means

\[\widehat{DiD} = (\bar y_{NJ,\text{after}} - \bar y_{NJ,\text{before}}) - (\bar y_{PA,\text{after}} - \bar y_{PA,\text{before}})\]

Code 
m <- with(
  stores,
  rbind(
    `New Jersey` = c(
      before = mean(fte1[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
      after = mean(fte2[nj == 1], na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    Pennsylvania = c(mean(fte1[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE), mean(fte2[nj == 0], na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)
cbind(m, change = m[, "after"] - m[, "before"])
               before    after     change
New Jersey   20.43941 21.02743  0.5880214
Pennsylvania 23.33117 21.16558 -2.1655844
Code 
did_hand <- diff(m["New Jersey", ]) - diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])
c(did = did_hand[[1]])
     did 
2.753606

In New Jersey a restaurant had 20.44 full-time equivalents before and 21.03 after the law: a small rise. In Pennsylvania employment fell, from 23.33 to 21.17. The difference in differences is +2.75 FTE per restaurant. The textbook theory of the labour market expects a minus.

Step 2: a regression

The same number is the coefficient of the product term in a regression with two indicator variables:

\[y_{it} = \alpha + \beta\,NJ_i + \gamma\,\text{After}_t + \delta\,(NJ_i \times \text{After}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}\]

\(\alpha\) is Pennsylvania before, \(\beta\) the difference between the states before, \(\gamma\) the change in Pennsylvania, and \(\delta\) the DiD. The regression also gives a standard error, but the two interviews of the same restaurant are not independent. So the errors are clustered by restaurant, here by hand:

\[V = \frac{G}{G-1}\,\frac{N-1}{N-K}\,(X^\top X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_g X_g^\top e_g e_g^\top X_g\Big)(X^\top X)^{-1}\]

Code 
long <- rbind(
  with(stores, data.frame(id, nj, after = 0, fte = fte1)),
  with(stores, data.frame(id, nj, after = 1, fte = fte2))
)
long <- subset(long, !is.na(fte))
fit <- lm(fte ~ nj * after, long)
X <- model.matrix(fit)
scores <- rowsum(X * residuals(fit), long$id)
G <- nrow(scores)
N <- nrow(X)
K <- ncol(X)
V <- G /
  (G - 1) *
  (N - 1) /
  (N - K) *
  solve(crossprod(X)) %*% crossprod(scores) %*% solve(crossprod(X))
clustered <- feols(fte ~ nj * after, long, cluster = ~ id)
rbind(
  estimate = c(
    lm = coef(fit)[["nj:after"]],
    by_hand = coef(fit)[["nj:after"]],
    feols = coef(clustered)[["nj:after"]]
  ),
  SE = c(
    sqrt(vcov(fit)["nj:after", "nj:after"]),
    sqrt(V["nj:after", "nj:after"]),
    se(clustered)[["nj:after"]]
  )
)
               lm  by_hand    feols
estimate 2.753606 2.753606 2.753606
SE       1.688409 1.306607 1.306607

The usual SE (1.69) is too large here. It does not know that a restaurant is compared with itself.

Step 3: changes, or two-way fixed effects

With two periods one can also take the change of each restaurant and compare the two groups with an ordinary regression. Or give every restaurant and every period its own constant (two-way fixed effects, TWFE, see panel data). For restaurants with both interviews that is the same:

Code 
both <- subset(stores, !is.na(fte1) & !is.na(fte2)); both$change <- both$fte2 - both$fte1
change_fit <- feols(change ~ nj, both, vcov = "hetero")
twfe_fit   <- feols(fte ~ nj:after | id + after, subset(long, id %in% both$id), cluster = ~ id)
v_hand <- with(
  both,
  sqrt(var(change[nj == 1]) / sum(nj == 1) + var(change[nj == 0]) / sum(nj == 0))
)
rbind(
  `regression of the changes` = c(estimate = coef(change_fit)[["nj"]], SE = se(change_fit)[["nj"]]),
  `two-way fixed effects` = c(coef(twfe_fit)[["nj:after"]], se(twfe_fit)[["nj:after"]]),
  `two means, by hand` = c(with(both, mean(change[nj == 1]) - mean(change[nj == 0])), v_hand)
)
                          estimate       SE
regression of the changes     2.75 1.337725
two-way fixed effects         2.75 1.337723
two means, by hand            2.75 1.342341

384 of the 410 restaurants have both values, and the result is 2.75 (SE 1.34).

Step 4: the assumption

What is the causal effect? The outcome of New Jersey after the law, minus what it would have been without it. The second part nobody has seen. DiD fills it in: New Jersey would have changed like Pennsylvania. That is the parallel trends assumption:

\[E[y_{\text{after}}(0) - y_{\text{before}}(0) \mid NJ] = E[y_{\text{after}}(0) - y_{\text{before}}(0) \mid PA]\]

(\(y(0)\): employment without the law.)

Code 
lines <- data.frame(
  state = rep(c("New Jersey", "Pennsylvania", "New Jersey without the law (assumed)"), each = 2),
  time = rep(0:1, 3),
  fte = c(
    m["New Jersey", ],
    m["Pennsylvania", ],
    m["New Jersey", "before"],
    m["New Jersey", "before"] + diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])
  )
)
ggplot(lines, aes(time, fte, colour = state, linetype = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 0:1,
    labels = c("February 1992", "November 1992"),
    limits = c(-0.1, 1.15)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "New Jersey" = "#2a78d6",
      "Pennsylvania" = "#eb6834",
      "New Jersey without the law (assumed)" = "#2a78d6"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "New Jersey" = "solid",
      "Pennsylvania" = "solid",
      "New Jersey without the law (assumed)" = "dashed"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 1.06,
    xend = 1.06,
    y = lines$fte[6],
    yend = lines$fte[2],
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.09, y = mean(lines$fte[c(2, 6)]), label = "DiD", hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "The four means, and what the assumption adds",
    x = NULL,
    y = "full-time equivalents per restaurant"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")

Note where the result comes from. New Jersey hardly moved. The effect is mostly the fall in Pennsylvania, which New Jersey is supposed to have been spared.

The law is estimated to have raised employment by 2.75 FTE per restaurant, 95% CI [0.19, 5.32], p = .036. That is 13% of the 20.4 before the law. Whether it is a rise or nothing is one question. That the interval excludes a loss is what started the debate.

5. Other ways of looking

More than one comparison

Pennsylvania need not be the only comparison. In New Jersey some restaurants already paid $5 or more. The law meant nothing to them. Card and Krueger used the gap: by how much a restaurant had to raise its starting wage to reach the new minimum.

Code 
stores$gap <- with(stores, ifelse(nj == 0, 0, pmax(0, (5.05 - wage_st) / wage_st)))
both$gap <- stores$gap[match(both$id, stores$id)]
gap_all <- feols(change ~ gap, both, vcov = "hetero")
gap_nj <- feols(change ~ gap, subset(both, nj == 1), vcov = "hetero")
both$wage_group <- cut(
  both$wage_st,
  c(0, 4.251, 4.999, 10),
  labels = c("4.25", "4.26 to 4.99", "5.00 or more")
)
within <- with(
  subset(both, nj == 1 & !is.na(wage_group)),
  data.frame(
    starting_wage_before = levels(wage_group),
    restaurants = as.numeric(table(wage_group)),
    mean_before = as.numeric(tapply(fte1, wage_group, mean)),
    mean_change = as.numeric(tapply(change, wage_group, mean)),
    se = as.numeric(tapply(change, wage_group, function(v) sd(v) / sqrt(length(v))))
  )
)

In New Jersey, employment changed by 1.20 in the restaurants that paid $4.25, and by -2.16 in those that already paid $5. The slope on the gap (with both states) times the mean gap in New Jersey (0.10) is 1.72 FTE: the same sign as the DiD, and smaller. Two different control groups tell the same story. That is better evidence than one. (But the restaurants that already paid well were also larger before the law, 22.2 FTE against 19.4, like those in Pennsylvania. Section 6 comes back to this.)

Other outcomes, other definitions

Code

  d <- data.frame(nj = stores$nj, change = b - a)
  f <- feols(change ~ nj, d, vcov = "hetero")

}
fte_w <- function(weight) {
  change_in(
    with(stores, empft + nmgrs + weight * emppt),
    with(stores, empft2 + nmgrs2 + weight * emppt2)

}

6. How far can we trust it?

The trends

With several periods before the law, one could look whether the two states moved together. Here there are only two interviews, so parallel trends cannot be checked at all. What one can do is to ask how wrong the assumption must be (the idea is developed by Rambachan & Roth, 2023). If New Jersey would have changed by \(d\) FTE more than Pennsylvania without any law, the effect is \(\widehat{DiD} - d\):

Code 
est <- coef(clustered)[["nj:after"]]; se_cl <- se(clustered)[["nj:after"]]
cbind(
  value = c(
    d_that_removes_the_significance = est - 1.96 * se_cl,
    d_that_removes_the_effect = est,
    change_in_Pennsylvania = diff(m["Pennsylvania", ])[[1]]
  )
)
                                    value
d_that_removes_the_significance  0.192656
d_that_removes_the_effect        2.753606
change_in_Pennsylvania          -2.165584

A difference in trends of only 0.19 FTE takes the interval to zero, and one of 2.75 takes the whole effect away. The change in Pennsylvania was -2.17.

Two states are two observations

The standard error counted 410 restaurants. But the law was given to states, and there are two. Suppose each state had a shock of its own in 1992 (weather, the local economy), with a standard deviation \(\sigma\) in the change per restaurant. Then the variance of the DiD is the one from the restaurants plus \(2\sigma^2\) (Donald & Lang, 2007):

Code 
sig <- seq(0, 2, length.out = 100); sdw <- sqrt(se_cl^2 + 2 * sig^2)
ggplot(data.frame(sig, lo = est - 1.96 * sdw, hi = est + 1.96 * sdw), aes(sig)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = est, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "95% interval of the DiD, if states have shocks of their own",
    x = "standard deviation of the shock of a state (FTE per restaurant)",
    y = "DiD"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
sigma_limit <- sqrt(((est / 1.96)^2 - se_cl^2) / 2)
interval1 <- est + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(se_cl^2 + 2)
cbind(
  value = c(
    sigma_at_which_the_interval_reaches_zero = sigma_limit,
    low_if_sigma_1 = interval1[1],
    high_if_sigma_1 = interval1[2]
  )
)
                                              value
sigma_at_which_the_interval_reaches_zero  0.3650511
low_if_sigma_1                           -1.0202071
high_if_sigma_1                           6.5274187

Shocks with an SD of 0.37 FTE (1.8% of a restaurant’s staff) are enough to take the significance away. And nothing in the data can tell us how large they are, because each state was seen once. With an SD of 1 the interval is [-1.0, 6.5]. A large loss of jobs is still hard to reconcile with the data; a small one is not. This is the general lesson of Bertrand et al. (2004) as well: cluster at the level at which the treatment was given, and have many such clusters.

Were the groups alike?

The restaurants in Pennsylvania were larger at the first interview (23.3 against 20.4). Large ones tend to shrink, and small ones to grow, if only because an interview catches a busy or a quiet week (regression to the mean). One could adjust for the first value:

Code 
ancova <- feols(fte2 ~ nj + fte1, both, vcov = "hetero")
rbind(
  `difference in differences` = c(estimate = coef(change_fit)[["nj"]], SE = se(change_fit)[["nj"]]),
  `adjusted for the first value` = c(coef(ancova)[["nj"]], se(ancova)[["nj"]])
)
                             estimate       SE
difference in differences    2.750000 1.337725
adjusted for the first value 1.338523 0.992067
Code 
c(
  slope_of_the_first_value = coef(ancova)[["fte1"]],
  correlation_of_the_two_interviews = with(both, cor(fte1, fte2))
)
         slope_of_the_first_value correlation_of_the_two_interviews 
                        0.5214388                         0.5537823

With the first value as a control, the effect is 1.34 (SE 0.99). The two methods answer with different assumptions: DiD says that the states differ permanently, and that the difference would have stayed the same; the other says that a restaurant with 20 FTE in New Jersey and one with 20 in Pennsylvania would have had the same future. DiD forces the slope of the first value to be 1; the data say 0.52. Neither is right by itself. (The conflict is known as Lord’s paradox.)

What others found

Neumark and Wascher (2000) collected payroll records of restaurants in the same two states and found a loss of jobs in New Jersey. Card and Krueger (2000) answered with official payroll records: employment grew as fast in New Jersey as in Pennsylvania, or slightly faster. How good the interview data are was a part of that debate.

7. When the treatment comes in waves

Laws rarely come in one place and on one day. Some states raise the wage in 1990, some in 1994, some never. For twenty years people ran one regression with unit and time effects and a treatment indicator (TWFE) on such data. If the effect grows with time or differs between places, that is wrong (Goodman-Bacon, 2021): the regression also uses places that were treated early as controls for those treated late. A simulation where we know the truth:

Code 
set.seed(231); n_unit <- 300; n_time <- 10
panel <- expand.grid(t = 1:n_time, id = 1:n_unit)
# treated from period 4, from period 8, never
panel$first <- rep(c(4, 8, 0), each = n_unit / 3)[panel$id]
panel$treated <- as.numeric(panel$first > 0 & panel$t >= panel$first)
# grows each year; faster in the early group
panel$effect <- panel$treated * ifelse(panel$first == 4, 1, 0.3) * (panel$t - panel$first + 1)
unit_level <- rnorm(n_unit, 0, 2) + ifelse(rep(c(4, 8, 0), each = n_unit / 3) == 4, 2, 0)
time_level <- cumsum(rnorm(n_time, 0.2, 0.5))
# parallel trends hold exactly
panel$y <- unit_level[panel$id] + time_level[panel$t] + panel$effect + rnorm(nrow(panel))
truth      <- mean(panel$effect[panel$treated == 1])
twfe       <- feols(y ~ treated | id + t, panel, cluster = ~ id)
twfe_no_never <- feols(y ~ treated | id + t, subset(panel, first > 0), cluster = ~ id)
c(
  true_mean_effect = truth,
  TWFE = coef(twfe)[["treated"]],
  TWFE_without_the_never_treated = coef(twfe_no_never)[["treated"]]
)
              true_mean_effect                           TWFE TWFE_without_the_never_treated 
                    2.98000000                     1.51468484                    -0.07322945

The true mean effect is 2.98. Every single effect is positive, and the trends are exactly parallel. TWFE says 1.51, and without the group that was never treated even -0.07.

The remedy (Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021) is to go back to the simple idea of step 1. For every group \(g\) and every period \(t\), do one DiD: with the period before the group’s treatment as “before”, and the never-treated as controls. Then average:

\[ATT(g, t) = (\bar y_{g,t} - \bar y_{g,g-1}) - (\bar y_{\text{never},t} - \bar y_{\text{never},g-1})\]

Code 
ym <- function(g, t) mean(panel$y[panel$first == g & panel$t == t])
att <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(4, 8), function(g) {
    data.frame(
      group = g,
      t = g:n_time,
      by_hand = sapply(g:n_time, function(t) (ym(g, t) - ym(g, g - 1)) - (ym(0, t) - ym(0, g - 1))),
      truth = sapply(g:n_time, function(t) mean(panel$effect[panel$first == g & panel$t == t]))
    )
  })
)
cs <- did::att_gt(
  yname = "y",
  tname = "t",
  idname = "id",
  gname = "first",
  data = panel,
  control_group = "nevertreated",
  bstrap = FALSE,
  cband = FALSE,
  base_period = "universal"
)
att$did_package <- cs$att[match(paste(att$group, att$t), paste(cs$group, cs$t))]
print(round(att, 2), row.names = FALSE)
