item.title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
item.description: Neural network regression in R with nnet, on 9,568 hours of a power plant (UCI): what a neuron is, how bent lines add up to any curve, the loss with weight decay, backpropagation written by hand and checked against numerical derivatives, the same minimum as nnet, two classic mistakes, many starts and many different answers, overfitting on forty rows, choosing the size with cross-validation, why random folds flatter methods that remember, a comparison with a straight line, a GAM, nearest neighbours and a random forest on conditions that were left out, what the network has learned, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Neural network regression in R with nnet, on 9,568 hours of a power plant (UCI): what a neuron is, how bent lines add up to any curve, the loss with weight decay, backpropagation written by hand and checked against numerical derivatives, the same minimum as nnet, two classic mistakes, many starts and many different answers, overfitting on forty rows, choosing the size with cross-validation, why random folds flatter methods that remember, a comparison with a straight line, a GAM, nearest neighbours and a random forest on conditions that were left out, what the network has learned, and APA reporting.

The question: many bent lines

A straight line is the wrong shape for most things. Splines bend it, one predictor at a time. A neural network goes further: it adds up many little bent lines, each of which looks at all predictors at once, and it finds out by itself where to bend and which predictors to combine.

That sounds like magic and is ordinary regression: there are parameters (called weights), there is a sum of squared errors, and a computer makes the sum small. The site’s page about handwritten digits uses networks to sort things into classes. Here the network predicts a number: the electrical power of a plant from the weather.

This page writes a network by hand, derivatives included, and finds the same solution as the package. Then it asks the question that matters more than the method: what is a fair test? The answer changes the ranking of the methods.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(nnet)        # nnet(): networks with one hidden layer (comes with R)
library(mgcv)        # bam(): a GAM, to compare with
# also used, with package::function: readxl (read_excel), ranger (ranger), FNN (knn.reg)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

1. The data

Code 
zip_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file(
  "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/294/combined+cycle+power+plant.zip",
  zip_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
files <- unzip(zip_file, exdir = tempfile("ccpp"))
raw   <- as.data.frame(readxl::read_excel(grep("xlsx$", files, value = TRUE), sheet = 1))
names(raw) <- c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity", "power")
c(rows = nrow(raw), exact_copies = sum(duplicated(raw)))
        rows exact_copies 
        9568           41
Code 
plant <- unique(raw)
summary(plant)
  temperature        vacuum         pressure         humidity          power      
 Min.   : 1.81   Min.   :25.36   Min.   : 992.9   Min.   : 25.56   Min.   :420.3  
 1st Qu.:13.53   1st Qu.:41.74   1st Qu.:1009.1   1st Qu.: 63.38   1st Qu.:439.8  
 Median :20.35   Median :52.08   Median :1012.9   Median : 75.00   Median :451.5  
 Mean   :19.66   Mean   :54.29   Mean   :1013.2   Mean   : 73.33   Mean   :454.3  
 3rd Qu.:25.71   3rd Qu.:66.51   3rd Qu.:1017.2   3rd Qu.: 84.85   3rd Qu.:468.4  
 Max.   :37.11   Max.   :81.56   Max.   :1033.3   Max.   :100.16   Max.   :495.8

The data come from a combined cycle power plant (Tüfekci, 2014; Tüfekci & Kaya, 2014), in which gas turbines and a steam turbine work together. Each row is the average of one hour at full load, between 2006 and 2011. The outcome is the net electrical power (MW). The predictors are the temperature of the air (°C), the pressure of the air (mbar), the relative humidity (%), and the exhaust vacuum of the steam turbine (cm Hg). 41 rows are exact copies of others; we drop them, so that no row can be in the training data and in the test at once. 9,527 are left.

Two details of this file will matter later. The file has been shuffled, and there is no date. And the vacuum takes only 634 different values, although it is given with two decimals.

2. Look at the data

Code 
set.seed(201); some <- plant[sample(nrow(plant), 2000), ]
long <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity"), function(v) {
    data.frame(predictor = v, x = some[[v]], power = some$power)
  })
)
ggplot(long, aes(x, power)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Power against each predictor",
    subtitle = "2,000 of the hours",
    x = NULL,
    y = "power (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
round(cor(plant), 2)
            temperature vacuum pressure humidity power
temperature        1.00   0.84    -0.51    -0.54 -0.95
vacuum             0.84   1.00    -0.42    -0.31 -0.87
pressure          -0.51  -0.42     1.00     0.10  0.52
humidity          -0.54  -0.31     0.10     1.00  0.39
power             -0.95  -0.87     0.52     0.39  1.00

Warm air is thin, and a gas turbine gets less of it: temperature alone has a correlation of -0.95 with power. The relationship is nearly straight, with a bend. So a straight line will already do well, and a network can only win by details.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: standardise

Every variable gets mean 0 and SD 1 (with the mean and SD of the training data). Weights of different predictors then have comparable sizes, and the search starts in a sensible region.

Code 
standardise <- function(train, d) as.data.frame(scale(d, colMeans(train), apply(train, 2, sd)))
z <- standardise(plant, plant)
X <- as.matrix(z[, c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity")]); y <- z$power

Step 2: one neuron

A neuron takes a weighted sum of the predictors and sends it through an S-shaped function, the logistic function \(\sigma(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-u})\), the one from logistic regression:

\[h = \sigma(a_0 + a_1 x_1 + \dots + a_K x_K)\]

It is flat on the left, flat on the right and rises in between. The weights decide where the rise is, how steep, and in which direction.

Step 3: the network

The hidden layer has \(J\) neurons. The output is a linear regression on them:

\[\hat y = b_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{J} b_j\, \sigma\!\Big(a_{0j} + \sum_{k=1}^K a_{kj} x_k\Big)\]

That makes \(J(K + 1) + J + 1\) weights: with 4 predictors and 10 neurons, 61. Already a few S-curves add up to all kinds of shapes:

Code 
x1 <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200)
parts <- data.frame(
  x = rep(x1, 3),
  h = c(1.6 * plogis(-4 + 6 * x1), -2.2 * plogis(1 + 3 * x1), 1.5 * plogis(5 + 4 * x1)),
  neuron = rep(paste("neuron", 1:3), each = 200)
)
ggplot(parts, aes(x, h)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = neuron), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x1, h = tapply(parts$h, rep(1:200, 3), sum)), linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three neurons (dashed) and their sum (black)", x = "x", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

With enough neurons such a sum can come as close as you like to any continuous function (Hornik et al., 1989). That is a statement about what is possible. It does not say how many neurons or how much data you need, nor that the search will find it.

Step 4: the loss

As in least squares, with a penalty for large weights, called weight decay (\(\lambda\)). It is the penalty of ridge regression:

\[E(w) = \sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + \lambda \sum w^2\]

Step 5: the derivatives (backpropagation)

To go downhill one needs the slope of \(E\) in the direction of every weight. The chain rule gives it, from the output backwards (Rumelhart et al., 1986). With \(r_i = -2(y_i - \hat y_i)\) and the output of neuron \(j\) for row \(i\), \(h_{ij}\):

\[\frac{\partial E}{\partial b_j} = \sum_i r_i\, h_{ij} + 2\lambda b_j, \qquad \frac{\partial E}{\partial a_{kj}} = \sum_i \underbrace{r_i\, b_j\, h_{ij}(1 - h_{ij})}_{\text{the error of neuron } j}\, x_{ik} + 2\lambda a_{kj}\]

Code 
forward <- function(w, X, J) {
  # weights in the order that nnet uses
  K <- ncol(X)
  A <- matrix(w[1:(J * (K + 1))], K + 1)
  b <- w[-(1:(J * (K + 1)))]
  h <- plogis(cbind(1, X) %*% A)
  list(h = h, b = b, yhat = drop(cbind(1, h) %*% b))
}
loss <- function(w, X, y, J, decay) sum((y - forward(w, X, J)$yhat)^2) + decay * sum(w^2)
gradient <- function(w, X, y, J, decay) {
  f <- forward(w, X, J); r <- -2 * (y - f$yhat)
  neuron_error <- (r %o% f$b[-1]) * f$h * (1 - f$h)
  c(crossprod(cbind(1, X), neuron_error), crossprod(cbind(1, f$h), r)) + 2 * decay * w
}
set.seed(202)
w0 <- runif(2 * 5 + 3, -0.7, 0.7) # 2 neurons, 13 weights, a random start
numeric_slope <- sapply(seq_along(w0), function(i) {
  d <- replace(numeric(13), i, 1e-5)
  (loss(w0 + d, X, y, 2, 0.1) - loss(w0 - d, X, y, 2, 0.1)) / 2e-5
})
max(abs(numeric_slope / gradient(w0, X, y, 2, 0.1) - 1))                    # relative difference
[1] 3.351439e-10

The formula and the numerical slopes agree. (Always do this check when you write derivatives yourself.)

Step 6: go downhill

R’s optimiser optim() does the walking. nnet() gets the same start, so that we can compare:

Code 
by_hand <- optim(
  w0,
  loss,
  gradient,
  X = X,
  y = y,
  J = 2,
  decay = 0.1,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 1000, abstol = 1e-4, reltol = 1e-8)
)
package <- nnet(X, y, size = 2, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, Wts = w0, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
cbind(
  value = c(
    loss_at_the_start = loss(w0, X, y, 2, 0.1),
    loss_by_hand = by_hand$value,
    loss_nnet = package$value,
    largest_difference_in_the_weights = max(abs(by_hand$par - package$wts))
  )
)
                                         value
loss_at_the_start                 1.928871e+04
loss_by_hand                      5.797301e+02
loss_nnet                         5.797300e+02
largest_difference_in_the_weights 1.312188e-04

The two arrive at the same place.

Two classic mistakes

Code 
set.seed(203)
forgot_scaling <- nnet(power ~ ., plant, size = 10, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
forgot_linout  <- nnet(power ~ ., z, size = 10, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
c(
  SD_of_power = sd(plant$power),
  RMSE_without_scaling = rmse(predict(forgot_scaling, plant), plant$power),
  RMSE_without_linout = sd(plant$power) * rmse(predict(forgot_linout, z), z$power)
)
         SD_of_power RMSE_without_scaling  RMSE_without_linout 
            17.03908             17.03819             17.03819
Code 
rbind(
  predictions_without_linout = range(predict(forgot_linout, z)),
  outcome_standardised = range(z$power)
)
                                [,1]     [,2]
predictions_without_linout  0.000000 0.000000
outcome_standardised       -1.999868 2.431122

Without standardising, the weighted sums are in the thousands, every neuron is stuck on its flat part, and the network predicts the mean (RMSE 17.0 MW, the SD of power). Without linout = TRUE the output itself goes through the S-function and cannot leave the interval from 0 to 1; here every prediction is 0. No error message in either case.

4. Different starts, different answers

A network has many minima. First on forty rows, with temperature as the only predictor, so that we can see the curves:

Code 
set.seed(204)
forty <- z[sample(nrow(z), 40), ]
grid <- data.frame(temperature = seq(-2.6, 2.9, length.out = 300))
curves <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0, 0.1), function(dc) {
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:4, function(s) {
        set.seed(s)
        m <- nnet(
          power ~ temperature,
          forty,
          size = 15,
          decay = dc,
          linout = TRUE,
          trace = FALSE,
          maxit = 2000
        )
        data.frame(
          temperature = grid$temperature,
          power = drop(predict(m, grid)),
          start = s,
          train_rmse = rmse(predict(m, forty), forty$power),
          setting = ifelse(dc == 0, "no decay", "decay 0.1")
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
back <- function(v, name) v * sd(plant[[name]]) + mean(plant[[name]])
ggplot(
  curves,
  aes(back(temperature, "temperature"), back(power, "power"), group = start, colour = factor(start))
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    data = forty,
    aes(back(temperature, "temperature"), back(power, "power")),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~setting) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(415, 505)) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "15 neurons on 40 hours, four random starts each",
    x = "temperature (°C)",
    y = "power (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
aggregate(train_rmse ~ setting, curves, function(v) round(range(v) * sd(plant$power), 2))
    setting train_rmse.1 train_rmse.2
1 decay 0.1         3.95         3.95
2  no decay         1.58         2.46

With 46 weights and 40 points the network without decay runs through the gaps as it likes: four starts, four curves, and the differences are largest where there are few data. A little decay makes the four curves the same. Now with all rows and all predictors:

Code 
fits <- lapply(1:6, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  nnet(power ~ ., z, size = 10, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 600)
})
loss_values <- sapply(fits, function(m) m$value)
preds <- sapply(fits, function(m) back(drop(predict(m, z)), "power"))
round(loss_values, 1)
[1] 542.3 544.7 545.7 544.7 542.4 545.8
Code 
cbind(
  value = c(
    largest_difference_in_a_weight = max(apply(sapply(fits, function(m) m$wts), 1, function(v) {
      diff(range(v))
    })),
    typical_SD_between_the_predictions = mean(apply(preds, 1, sd)),
    RMSE_of_the_first = rmse(preds[, 1], plant$power)
  )
)
                                       value
largest_difference_in_a_weight     5.9772949
typical_SD_between_the_predictions 0.4560367
RMSE_of_the_first                  4.0272418

Six starts end at different places (loss between 542.3 and 545.8), with quite different weights. But the predictions differ by only 0.46 MW on average. So single weights mean nothing, and nobody should interpret them. The predictions are what one can use. Averaging the predictions of several networks (an ensemble) makes them more stable; section 6 shows by how much.

5. What is a fair test?

How many neurons? The usual recipe is cross-validation with random folds. But look at the data again. 99.5% of the rows share their value of the vacuum, to two decimals, with other rows: 634 values in 9,527 hours. The most likely explanation is that the vacuum was recorded less often than the rest, and that rows with the same value come from the same period. The file does not say, and its order is destroyed. But if so, then random folds put hours of the same period in the training data and in the test. A method that remembers its neighbours would be rewarded for remembering.

So we use two kinds of folds: random rows, and whole groups of rows with the same vacuum, so that the test has conditions that the model has never seen.

Code 
set.seed(205)
group   <- as.integer(factor(plant$vacuum)); n_group <- max(group)
folds3 <- list(
  random = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = nrow(plant))),
  `new conditions` = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n_group))[group]
)
net_predict <- function(train, test, size, decay, starts = 1, maxit = 400) {
  a <- standardise(train, train)
  b <- standardise(train, test)
  p <- sapply(starts, function(s) {
    set.seed(s)
    drop(predict(
      nnet(
        power ~ .,
        a,
        size = size,
        decay = decay,
        linout = TRUE,
        trace = FALSE,
        maxit = maxit,
        MaxNWts = 5000
      ),
      b
    ))
  })
  mean(train$power) + sd(train$power) * p
}
grid <- expand.grid(size = c(2, 5, 10, 20), decay = c(0.01, 0.1, 1))
cv <- do.call(
  cbind,
  lapply(folds3, function(f) {
    sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
      e <- numeric(nrow(plant))
      for (k in 1:3) {
        e[f == k] <- net_predict(plant[f != k, ], plant[f == k, ], grid$size[i], grid$decay[i])[,
          1
        ] -
          plant$power[f == k]
      }
      sqrt(mean(e^2))
    })
  })
)
print(round(cbind(grid, cv), 3), row.names = FALSE)
 size decay random new conditions
    2  0.01  4.203          4.251
    5  0.01  4.167          4.277
   10  0.01  4.048          4.306
   20  0.01  3.970          4.368
    2  0.10  4.202          4.251
    5  0.10  4.169          4.272
   10  0.10  4.066          4.300
   20  0.10  4.015          4.322
    2  1.00  4.213          4.271
    5  1.00  4.202          4.286
   10  1.00  4.198          4.280
   20  1.00  4.184          4.276
Code 
cv_long <- data.frame(
  size = rep(grid$size, 2),
  decay = factor(rep(grid$decay, 2)),
  rmse = as.vector(cv),
  folds = rep(colnames(cv), each = nrow(grid))
)
ggplot(cv_long, aes(size, rmse, colour = decay)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~folds) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(2, 5, 10, 20)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")) +
  labs(
    title = "Error of the network against its size, for two kinds of folds",
    x = "neurons",
    y = "RMSE (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
best_r <- grid[which.min(cv[, "random"]), ]; best_g <- grid[which.min(cv[, "new conditions"]), ]
rbind(
  random = cbind(best_r, rmse = min(cv[, "random"])),
  `new conditions` = cbind(best_g, rmse = min(cv[, "new conditions"]))
)
               size decay     rmse
random           20  0.01 3.969926
new conditions    2  0.10 4.250756

With random folds the larger networks keep getting better, and the best has 20 neurons and a decay of 0.01. With new conditions they get worse, unless a strong decay holds them back, and the best has 2 neurons. All settings lie between 4.25 and 4.37 MW. What the larger networks gained with random folds was mostly memory of the vacuum values in the data.

6. The network against others

Both kinds of folds again, with new folds, for seven methods: a straight line, a GAM, the 5 nearest neighbours, a random forest, the small network that the second kind of folds chose (2 neurons, decay 0.1), the large one that random folds chose (20 neurons, decay 0.01), and the average of three such large networks.

Code 
set.seed(206)
folds5 <- list(
  `random folds` = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(plant))),
  `new conditions` = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_group))[group]
)
methods <- function(train, test) {
  zt <- standardise(train, train)
  zn <- standardise(train, test)
  large <- net_predict(train, test, best_r$size, best_r$decay, starts = 1:3)
  cbind(
    `straight line` = predict(lm(power ~ ., train), test),
    GAM = as.numeric(predict(
      bam(power ~ s(temperature) + s(vacuum) + s(pressure) + s(humidity), data = train),
      test
    )),
    `nearest neighbours` = FNN::knn.reg(zt[, 1:4], zn[, 1:4], train$power, k = 5)$pred,
    `random forest` = predict(
      ranger::ranger(power ~ ., train, num.trees = 300, seed = 1),
      test
    )$predictions,
    `small network` = net_predict(train, test, best_g$size, best_g$decay)[, 1],
    `large network` = large[, 1],
    `3 large networks, averaged` = rowMeans(large)
  )
}
results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(folds5), function(kind) {
    f <- folds5[[kind]]
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:5, function(k) {
        p <- methods(plant[f != k, ], plant[f == k, ])
        data.frame(
          folds = kind,
          fold = k,
          method = colnames(p),
          rmse = apply(p, 2, rmse, plant$power[f == k]),
          mse = apply(p, 2, function(v) sum((v - plant$power[f == k])^2))
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
total <- aggregate(mse ~ method + folds, results, sum); total$rmse <- sqrt(total$mse / nrow(plant))
wide <- reshape(
  total[, c("method", "folds", "rmse")],
  idvar = "method",
  timevar = "folds",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(wide) <- c("method", "new", "random")
wide <- wide[order(wide$new), ]
print(
  data.frame(
    method = wide$method,
    random_folds = round(wide$random, 2),
    new_conditions = round(wide$new, 2)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
                     method random_folds new_conditions
 3 large networks, averaged         3.90           4.21
              small network         4.20           4.23
                        GAM         4.17           4.24
              large network         3.96           4.33
              random forest         3.22           4.43
              straight line         4.56           4.58
         nearest neighbours         3.79           4.80
Code 
results$method <- factor(results$method, levels = rev(wide$method[order(wide$random)]))
ggplot(results, aes(rmse, method)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = transform(total, method = factor(method, levels = levels(results$method))),
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~folds) +
  labs(
    title = "Error of seven methods, two kinds of folds",
    subtitle = "Orange: all rows. Blue: single folds",
    x = "RMSE (MW)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
Code 
w  <- function(m, v) wide[[v]][wide$method == m]
by_fold <- function(m) subset(results, folds == "new conditions" & method == m)$rmse
cbind(
  value = c(
    folds_in_which_the_small_network_beats_the_forest = sum(
      by_fold("small network") < by_fold("random forest")
    ),
    folds_in_which_the_average_beats_one_large_network = sum(
      by_fold("3 large networks, averaged") < by_fold("large network")
    )
  )
)
                                                   value
folds_in_which_the_small_network_beats_the_forest      4
folds_in_which_the_average_beats_one_large_network     4
  • With random folds the random forest wins by far: 3.22 MW, against 3.90 for the averaged large networks, 4.17 for the GAM and 4.56 for the straight line. (In the paper that introduced the data, bagged trees came first among many methods, with an RMSE of 3.79 MW and folds of shuffled rows; Tüfekci, 2014.)
  • With new conditions the order is another one. The averaged large networks (4.21), the small network (4.23) and the GAM (4.24) are practically tied; the forest has 4.43, the straight line 4.58. The small network beats the forest in 4 of the 5 folds. The nearest neighbours, which were well ahead of the straight line before, are the last with 4.80.
  • The stiff methods (straight line, GAM, small network) have nearly the same error in both tests, for example 4.17 and 4.24 for the GAM. They cannot remember single periods. The flexible ones lose a lot: the forest goes from 3.22 to 4.43, the large network from 3.96 to 4.33.
  • Averaging three large networks changed the error from 4.33 to 4.21 (new conditions) and from 3.96 to 3.90 (random folds): it helped, at three times the cost.

Which of the two tests is right? It depends on the use. To fill a missing hour in the past, random folds. To forecast the power of next week, the second, and even that may be too kind, since vacuum values close to the left-out ones are still in the training data. Choose the folds so that the test is like the use.

The gain from all that flexibility is modest here. From the straight line to the best method with new conditions, the RMSE falls from 4.58 to 4.21 MW.

7. What has the network learned?

The partial dependence of a predictor: set it to a value in every row, predict, and average. For three large networks, the small one and the GAM:

Code 
set.seed(207); bg <- plant[sample(nrow(plant), 400), ]; zbg <- standardise(plant, bg)
one_net <- function(size, decay, s) {
  set.seed(s)
  nnet(power ~ ., z, size = size, decay = decay, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
}
nets <- c(
  lapply(1:3, function(s) one_net(best_r$size, best_r$decay, s)),
  list(one_net(best_g$size, best_g$decay, 1))
)
gam_all <- bam(power ~ s(temperature) + s(vacuum) + s(pressure) + s(humidity), data = plant)
pd <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity"), function(v) {
    q <- seq(quantile(plant[[v]], 0.01), quantile(plant[[v]], 0.99), length.out = 25)
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(q, function(x0) {
        b2 <- bg
        b2[[v]] <- x0
        zb <- standardise(plant, b2)
        data.frame(
          predictor = v,
          x = x0,
          model = c(paste("large", 1:3), "small", "GAM"),
          power = c(
            sapply(nets, function(m) mean(back(drop(predict(m, zb)), "power"))),
            mean(predict(gam_all, b2))
          )
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
pd$kind <- factor(
  ifelse(
    grepl("large", pd$model),
    "three large networks",
    ifelse(pd$model == "small", "small network", "GAM")
  ),
  levels = c("three large networks", "small network", "GAM")
)
ggplot(pd, aes(x, power, group = model, colour = kind, linewidth = kind)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(0.5, 1, 1), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence of power on each predictor", x = NULL, y = "power (MW)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
span <- function(v, m) { p <- subset(pd, predictor == v & model == m); diff(range(p$power)) }
spans <- sapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "humidity", "pressure"), function(v) {
  sapply(c("small", "GAM", "large 1"), function(m) span(v, m))
})
round(spans, 1)
        temperature vacuum humidity pressure
small          50.9   11.3      6.3      4.4
GAM            48.3   10.3      6.7      2.9
large 1        42.5   15.0      7.2      2.5

In the small network, temperature moves the power by 50.9 MW over its range (from the 1st to the 99th percentile), the vacuum by 11.3, humidity by 6.3 and air pressure by 4.4. The GAM draws nearly the same curves. The three large networks agree with them in the middle and fan out at the ends, where rows are few and where partial dependence asks for combinations that hardly occur (a cold hour with a high vacuum). When a network and a GAM show the same picture, the GAM is the better story: it can be written down, and it comes with intervals.

8. Things to keep in mind

  • Standardise the predictors and the outcome, with the means and SDs of the training data. In R’s nnet() add linout = TRUE for a number.
  • Try several starts, set the seed, and average the predictions.
  • Use decay (or stop early). With enough of it the exact number of neurons matters little.
  • Choose with folds that look like the use: groups, sites, times, persons.
  • Small tables: for a few thousand rows and a handful of predictors, trees (random forest, boosting), GAMs and Gaussian processes are usually as good and less work. Networks pay off with images, sound, text and very many rows.
  • Deeper networks have several hidden layers and other functions (ReLU instead of \(\sigma\)), and are trained on small batches with packages such as torch or keras3. The principles on this page are the same.
  • Outside the data S-curves become flat, so the network predicts a constant. It never says that it does not know. (Gaussian processes do, with the limits shown there.)
  • No intervals and no tests come with it. Use the bootstrap, ensembles or conformal prediction for intervals.
  • Weights are not effects. Report partial dependence instead, and remember that predictors that belong together (temperature and vacuum, r = 0.84) make partial dependence an average over combinations that never occur.

9. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the data and any dropped rows, the standardisation, the architecture and the number of weights, the loss, decay, optimiser and number of starts, how the settings were chosen, how the test was made, and the comparison with simple models. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
apa_table <- data.frame(Method = wide$method, random = f2(wide$random), new = f2(wide$new))
n_weights <- function(size) size * 6 + 1

Method (data analysis):

The net hourly electrical power of a combined cycle power plant (N = 9,527 hours at full load, after removing 41 exact duplicates; Tüfekci, 2014) was predicted from air temperature, air pressure, relative humidity and exhaust vacuum. Neural networks with one hidden layer (logistic units, linear output) were fitted to standardised variables by minimising the sum of squared errors with a weight-decay penalty, with the quasi-Newton optimiser of the R package nnet (Venables & Ripley, 2002). Because the vacuum takes only 634 different values and hours with the same value probably come from the same period, cross-validation was done in two ways: with random folds and with folds of whole vacuum values. The number of hidden units (2–20) and the decay (0.01–1) were chosen by 3-fold cross-validation, which gave 20 units (121 weights) and a decay of 0.01 with random folds, and 2 units (13 weights) and a decay of 0.1 with folds of whole vacuum values. Both networks, the average of three large ones from different random starts, linear regression, a generalized additive model, 5-nearest neighbours, and a random forest were then compared with 5-fold cross-validation on new folds. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

With random folds, the random forest had the lowest root mean squared error (RMSE = 3.22 MW; Table 1). With folds of whole vacuum values, its error was 4.43 MW, and the average of three large networks (4.21 MW), the small network (4.23 MW) and the generalized additive model (4.24 MW) were more accurate, with practically the same error; linear regression had an error of 4.58 MW. A single large network went from 3.96 to 4.33 MW. In the small network, the partial dependence of power on temperature spanned 50.9 MW, on the vacuum 11.3 MW.

Table 1

Root Mean Squared Error (MW) of Seven Methods With Two Kinds of Cross-Validation

Method Random folds Folds of whole vacuum values
3 large networks, averaged 3.90 4.21
small network 4.20 4.23
GAM 4.17 4.24
large network 3.96 4.33
random forest 3.22 4.43
straight line 4.56 4.58
nearest neighbours 3.79 4.80

Note. N = 9,527. Five folds each, RMSE over all rows. Small network: 2 hidden units; large networks: 20.

Points to remember:

  • Report the size, the decay, the number of starts and the seeds.
  • Report a simple model next to the network.
  • Say how the folds were made, and why.
  • Do not interpret single weights.

10. Summary

When Many rows, many predictors, unknown shapes and interactions, prediction is the goal
The model \(\hat y = b_0 + \sum_j b_j\,\sigma(a_{0j} + \sum_k a_{kj}x_k)\)
Loss Squared errors plus \(\lambda\sum w^2\)
Derivatives Chain rule, backwards: backpropagation
Settings Number of neurons, decay; several starts; average
How (R) nnet::nnet(y ~ ., size = , decay = , linout = TRUE, maxit = ) on standardised data
Check Cross-validation with folds that look like the use; a simple model as comparison
Danger Not scaled, no linout, one start, random folds for grouped data
Related pages Splines and GAMs, Gaussian processes, nearest neighbours, handwritten digits

References

Hornik, K., Stinchcombe, M., & White, H. (1989). Multilayer feedforward networks are universal approximators. Neural Networks, 2(5), 359–366. https://doi.org/10.1016/0893-6080(89)90020-8

Rumelhart, D. E., Hinton, G. E., & Williams, R. J. (1986). Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Nature, 323(6088), 533–536. https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0

Tüfekci, P. (2014). Prediction of full load electrical power output of a base load operated combined cycle power plant using machine learning methods. International Journal of Electrical Power & Energy Systems, 60, 126–140. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijepes.2014.02.027

Tüfekci, P., & Kaya, H. (2014). Combined cycle power plant [Data set]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5002N

Venables, W. N., & Ripley, B. D. (2002). Modern applied statistics with S (4th ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-21706-2

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Gaussian Process Regression: CO₂ Again, With Error Bars That Grow
item.description: Gaussian process regression in R, written by hand in two short functions and checked with kernlab, on NOAA’s monthly CO₂ record: functions as random draws, kernels, conditioning on data, the marginal likelihood, adding kernels for trend, season and slow swings and taking them apart again, leave-one-out checks inside the data, forecasts of fifteen to twenty years from six starting dates, why the mean function and the kernel decide everything outside the data, what the error bars are worth, the cost, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Gaussian process regression in R, written by hand in two short functions and checked with kernlab, on NOAA’s monthly CO₂ record: functions as random draws, kernels, conditioning on data, the marginal likelihood, adding kernels for trend, season and slow swings and taking them apart again, leave-one-out checks inside the data, forecasts of fifteen to twenty years from six starting dates, why the mean function and the kernel decide everything outside the data, what the error bars are worth, the cost, and APA reporting.

The question: a curve that says how sure it is

Polynomial regression drew curves through the CO₂ record of Mauna Loa, and the curves parted ways as soon as they left the data. Each of them was drawn as a thin, confident line. Nothing in the method said: here I do not know.

Gaussian process regression (GP) is built the other way round. It starts with all the functions that seem reasonable: smooth ones, or wavy ones, or ones that repeat every year. Then it looks at the data and keeps those that pass near the points. Where there are data, the remaining functions agree, and the error bars are narrow. Where there are none, they spread out, and the error bars grow.

The model is completely described by two things: a mean function and a kernel, which says how similar the values at two times are expected to be. The whole calculation fits in two short functions. This page writes them, uses them on the CO₂ record, and checks whether the error bars can be believed. (Inside the data: yes. Outside: less than one would like.)

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)    # gausspr(), to check the code (and for everyday use)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

1. The data

Code 
raw <- read.csv("https://gml.noaa.gov/webdata/ccgg/trends/co2/co2_mm_mlo.csv", comment.char = "#")
co2 <- data.frame(year = raw$decimal.date, t = raw$decimal.date - 2000, ppm = raw$average)
past   <- subset(co2, year < 2007)            # what the model may see
future <- subset(co2, year >= 2007)           # the test: nearly twenty years
c(past = nrow(past), future = nrow(future))
  past future 
   586    238

The monthly means of CO₂ in parts per million (ppm), from NOAA (Lan & Keeling, 2026), as on the polynomial page: 586 months until the end of 2006 for learning, and 238 months since then for the test. t is the number of years since 2000.

2. The method step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a kernel is an opinion about functions

The squared exponential (or radial) kernel says that the values at two times \(t\) and \(t'\) are similar if the times are close:

\[k(t, t') = s^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{(t - t')^2}{2\ell^2}\right)\]

\(s\) is how far the function strays from its mean, \(\ell\) (the length scale) how far one must go until it has forgotten where it was. A Gaussian process with this kernel is a distribution over functions: the values at any set of times have a multivariate normal distribution, whose covariances are the kernel. So we can draw functions from it:

Code 
k_rbf <- function(a, b, s, l) s^2 * exp(-outer(a, b, "-")^2 / (2 * l^2))
draw  <- function(K, n) t(chol(K + 1e-8 * diag(nrow(K)))) %*% matrix(rnorm(nrow(K) * n), ncol = n)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 150); set.seed(171)
draws <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0.5, 2), function(l) {
    f <- draw(k_rbf(x, x, 1, l), 5)
    data.frame(
      x = rep(x, 5),
      f = as.vector(f),
      id = rep(1:5, each = length(x)),
      l = paste("length scale", l)
    )
  })
)
ggplot(draws, aes(x, f, group = id, colour = factor(id))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~l) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Functions drawn from a Gaussian process, before seeing any data",
    x = "t",
    y = "f(t)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

Step 2: condition on the data

We observe \(y_i = f(t_i) + \varepsilon_i\) with noise of variance \(\sigma^2\). Data and unknown values are jointly normal, so the rule for conditional normal distributions gives everything. With \(K\) the kernel matrix of the data, \(k_*\) the vector of kernels between the data and a new time \(t_*\):

\[\hat f(t_*) = k_*^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y, \qquad \text{Var}\,f(t_*) = k(t_*, t_*) - k_*^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} k_*\]

The mean is a weighted sum of the data. The variance starts from the prior variance and is reduced by what the data say. It does not depend on \(y\) at all, only on where the data are.

Code 
gp_fit <- function(t, y, kern, sigma) {
  L <- chol(kern(t, t) + sigma^2 * diag(length(t)))
  list(
    t = t,
    L = L,
    a = backsolve(L, backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)),
    kern = kern,
    sigma = sigma
  )
}
gp_predict <- function(m, new) {
  Ks <- m$kern(new, m$t)
  V <- backsolve(m$L, t(Ks), transpose = TRUE)
  list(mean = drop(Ks %*% m$a), sd = sqrt(pmax(diag(m$kern(new, new)) - colSums(V^2), 0)))
}
set.seed(172); t5 <- c(1, 2.2, 3, 6, 6.8); y5 <- sin(t5) + rnorm(5, 0, 0.1)
toy  <- gp_fit(t5, y5, function(a, b) k_rbf(a, b, 1, 1), 0.1)
pr   <- gp_predict(toy, x)
Kxx <- k_rbf(x, x, 1, 1)
post <- Kxx - k_rbf(x, t5, 1, 1) %*% solve(k_rbf(t5, t5, 1, 1) + 0.01 * diag(5), k_rbf(t5, x, 1, 1))
some <- pr$mean + draw(post + 1e-6 * diag(150), 5)
ggplot(
  data.frame(x, m = pr$mean, lo = pr$mean - 1.96 * pr$sd, hi = pr$mean + 1.96 * pr$sd),
  aes(x, m)
) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = data.frame(x = rep(x, 5), f = as.vector(some), id = rep(1:5, each = 150)),
    aes(x, f, group = id),
    colour = "grey60",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(t5, y5), aes(t5, y5), size = 2.6) +
  labs(
    title = "The same process after five observations",
    subtitle = "Blue: mean and 95% band. Grey: five functions that are still possible",
    x = "t",
    y = "f(t)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
check <- gausspr(
  matrix(t5),
  y5,
  kernel = "rbfdot",
  kpar = list(sigma = 1 / 2),
  var = 0.01,
  scaled = FALSE,
  fit = FALSE
) # kernlab's sigma is 1/(2 l^2)
max(abs(predict(check, matrix(x)) - pr$mean))
[1] 9.103829e-15

Between the points and beyond the last one, the functions disagree and the band opens. Far away the mean returns to the prior mean (0) and the band to the prior SD. kernlab gives the same curve.

Step 3: learn the kernel from the data

Where do \(s\), \(\ell\) and \(\sigma\) come from? From the marginal likelihood, the probability of the data with all possible functions averaged:

\[\log p(y) = -\tfrac12\, y^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y - \tfrac12 \log|K + \sigma^2 I| - \tfrac n2 \log 2\pi\]

The first term rewards fit, the second punishes a kernel that could explain anything. No cross-validation is needed for this trade-off.

Step 4: kernels can be added

The sum of two independent processes is a process whose kernel is the sum of the kernels. So we build a model from parts, each with its meaning (Roberts et al., 2013, show this for time series).

3. A kernel for CO₂

Rasmussen and Williams (2006) used this very record as an example. We use a simplified version of their kernel, with four parts:

Part Kernel Meaning
trend \(s_1^2 \exp(-r^2 / 2\ell_1^2)\) a smooth change over decades
season \(s_2^2 \exp(-r^2/2\ell_2^2 - 2\sin^2(\pi r)/p^2)\) repeats every year; its shape may change slowly
swings \(s_3^2 \exp(-r/\ell_3)\) irregular, some months to years, such as El Niño
noise \(\sigma^2\) on the diagonal single months

(\(r = |t - t'|\) in years.)

Code 
part <- function(a, b, th, which) {
  r <- abs(outer(a, b, "-"))
  switch(which, trend = th[["s1"]]^2 * exp(-r^2 / (2 * th[["l1"]]^2)),
         season = th[["s2"]]^2 * exp(-r^2 / (2 * th[["l2"]]^2) - 2 * sin(pi * r)^2 / th[["p"]]^2),
         swings = th[["s3"]]^2 * exp(-r / th[["l3"]]))
}
kernel <- function(a, b, th, parts) Reduce(`+`, lapply(parts, function(w) part(a, b, th, w)))
parts_A <- c("trend", "season", "swings")          # version A
parts_B <- c("season", "swings")                   # version B, with a mean function
H <- function(t) cbind(1, t, t^2)                  # the columns of that mean function
# marginal likelihood; H: columns of a mean function with unknown coefficients (estimated by
# generalized least squares)
neg_ml <- function(log_th, t, y, parts, H = NULL) {
  th <- as.list(exp(log_th)); K <- kernel(t, t, th, parts); diag(K) <- diag(K) + th$sigma^2
  L <- try(chol(K), silent = TRUE); if (inherits(L, "try-error")) return(1e6)
  z <- backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(H)) { A <- backsolve(L, H, transpose = TRUE); z <- qr.resid(qr(A), z) }
  sum(log(diag(L))) + sum(z^2) / 2 + length(y) / 2 * log(2 * pi)
}

Version A: no mean, everything in the kernel

The common default: subtract the overall mean and let the kernel do the rest.

Code 
start_A <- log(c(s1 = 60, l1 = 60, s2 = 3, l2 = 100, p = 1.3, s3 = 0.8, l3 = 2, sigma = 0.2))
opt_A <- optim(
  start_A,
  neg_ml,
  t = past$t,
  y = past$ppm - mean(past$ppm),
  parts = parts_A,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 80)
)
th_A  <- as.list(exp(opt_A$par))
round(unlist(th_A), 2)
    s1     l1     s2     l2      p     s3     l3  sigma 
 85.35  77.44   2.98 164.89   1.55   0.89   4.14   0.17

The length scale of the trend is 77.4 years, the season keeps its shape for a long time (\(\ell_2\) = 164.9 years), the swings have an SD of 0.89 ppm and the noise of single months is 0.17 ppm.

Version B: a quadratic mean, and the kernel for the rest

We know something that the kernel does not: the rise has been speeding up for a century. Give the process a mean function \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 t^2\) with unknown coefficients, and the kernels of the season and of the swings for the deviations from it:

Code 
start_B <- log(c(s2 = 3, l2 = 100, p = 1.3, s3 = 0.8, l3 = 2, sigma = 0.2))
opt_B <- optim(
  start_B,
  neg_ml,
  t = past$t,
  y = past$ppm,
  parts = parts_B,
  H = H(past$t),
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 80)
)
th_B  <- as.list(exp(opt_B$par))
round(unlist(th_B), 2)
    s2     l2      p     s3     l3  sigma 
  2.43 155.61   1.43   0.80   3.32   0.17

The prediction now has one more source of uncertainty, the coefficients of the mean. This is universal kriging, and it is generalized least squares for the \(\beta\)’s plus the GP for the residuals:

Code 
gp <- function(t, y, th, parts, H = NULL, new, H_new = NULL) {
  K <- kernel(t, t, th, parts)
  diag(K) <- diag(K) + th$sigma^2
  L <- chol(K)
  z <- backsolve(L, y, transpose = TRUE)
  Ks <- kernel(new, t, th, parts)
  V <- backsolve(L, t(Ks), transpose = TRUE)
  v <- rowSums(sapply(parts, function(w) diag(part(new, new, th, w)))) - colSums(V^2)
  if (is.null(H)) {
    return(list(mean = drop(crossprod(V, z)), sd = sqrt(pmax(v, 0) + th$sigma^2)))
  }
  A <- backsolve(L, H, transpose = TRUE)
  XtX <- solve(crossprod(A))
  beta <- XtX %*% crossprod(A, z)
  R <- H_new - crossprod(V, A) # what the mean adds that the data cannot fix
  list(
    mean = drop(H_new %*% beta + crossprod(V, z - A %*% beta)),
    sd = sqrt(pmax(v, 0) + rowSums((R %*% XtX) * R) + th$sigma^2),
    beta = drop(beta),
    beta_se = sqrt(diag(XtX))
  )
}

4. Inside the data

How well do the two versions predict single months of the past? Leave each month out and predict it from all the others. For a GP that needs no refitting. With \(Q = K_y^{-1} - K_y^{-1}H(H^\top K_y^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top K_y^{-1}\), where \(K_y = K + \sigma^2 I\) and \(H\) holds the columns of the mean function (without a mean function \(Q = K_y^{-1}\)):

\[y_i - \hat y_{-i} = \frac{[Qy]_i}{Q_{ii}}, \qquad \text{Var}_{-i} = \frac{1}{Q_{ii}}\]

Code 
loo <- function(t, y, th, parts, H = NULL) {
  K <- kernel(t, t, th, parts); diag(K) <- diag(K) + th$sigma^2; Q <- solve(K)
  if (!is.null(H)) { KH <- Q %*% H; Q <- Q - KH %*% solve(crossprod(H, KH), t(KH)) }
  data.frame(err = drop(Q %*% y) / diag(Q), sd = 1 / sqrt(diag(Q)))
}
loo_A <- loo(past$t, past$ppm - mean(past$ppm), th_A, parts_A)
loo_B <- loo(past$t, past$ppm, th_B, parts_B, H(past$t))
inside <- sapply(list(A = loo_A, B = loo_B), function(l) {
  c(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(l$err^2)),
    coverage_95 = mean(abs(l$err) < 1.96 * l$sd),
    coverage_50 = mean(abs(l$err) < 0.674 * l$sd)
  )
})
round(inside, 3)
                A     B
RMSE        0.237 0.237
coverage_95 0.949 0.949
coverage_50 0.532 0.531
Code 
c(log_marginal_likelihood_A = -opt_A$value, log_marginal_likelihood_B = -opt_B$value)
log_marginal_likelihood_A log_marginal_likelihood_B 
                -128.5221                 -117.2624

Single months are predicted to within 0.24 ppm by version A and 0.24 ppm by version B, and the 95% intervals contain 95% and 95% of them. Inside the data the two versions are the same, and their error bars can be believed. Only the marginal likelihood sees a difference (-117.3 for B against -128.5 for A).

5. The test: twenty years later

Code 
pA <- gp(past$t, past$ppm - mean(past$ppm), th_A, parts_A, new = future$t)
pA$mean <- pA$mean + mean(past$ppm)
pB <- gp(past$t, past$ppm, th_B, parts_B, H(past$t), future$t, H(future$t))
quad <- lm(
  ppm ~ t + I(t^2) + sin(2 * pi * t) + cos(2 * pi * t) + sin(4 * pi * t) + cos(4 * pi * t),
  data = past
) # the polynomial page, with a season
pQ <- predict(quad, future, interval = "prediction")
score <- function(m, lo, hi) {
  c(
    RMSE = rmse(m, future$ppm),
    coverage_95 = mean(future$ppm >= lo & future$ppm <= hi),
    mean_width = mean(hi - lo)
  )
}
scores <- rbind(
  `A: zero-mean GP` = score(pA$mean, pA$mean - 1.96 * pA$sd, pA$mean + 1.96 * pA$sd),
  `B: GP with a quadratic mean` = score(pB$mean, pB$mean - 1.96 * pB$sd, pB$mean + 1.96 * pB$sd),
  `quadratic regression + season (lm)` = score(pQ[, 1], pQ[, 2], pQ[, 3])
)
round(scores, 3)
                                    RMSE coverage_95 mean_width
A: zero-mean GP                    6.092       0.462      8.872
B: GP with a quadratic mean        1.579       1.000      5.903
quadratic regression + season (lm) 1.970       0.521      3.211
Code 
fc <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    year = future$year,
    m = pA$mean,
    lo = pA$mean - 1.96 * pA$sd,
    hi = pA$mean + 1.96 * pA$sd,
    model = "A: zero-mean GP"
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = future$year,
    m = pB$mean,
    lo = pB$mean - 1.96 * pB$sd,
    hi = pB$mean + 1.96 * pB$sd,
    model = "B: GP with a quadratic mean"
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = future$year,
    m = pQ[, 1],
    lo = pQ[, 2],
    hi = pQ[, 3],
    model = "quadratic regression + season"
  )
)
fc$obs <- rep(future$ppm, 3)
ggplot(fc, aes(year)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo - obs, ymax = hi - obs), fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = m - obs), colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#eb6834", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast from 2006 minus what was measured",
    subtitle = "Band: 95%. A good band contains the dashed zero line nearly always",
    x = NULL,
    y = "ppm"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
  • A, the zero-mean GP, is too low, by more and more: RMSE 6.1 ppm. Its band grows, as promised, and is still too narrow: it contains only 46% of the months, instead of 95%. Far from the data the trend kernel pulls the function back to the mean of 1958–2006. Nobody asked for that opinion; it came with the zero mean.
  • B, with a quadratic mean, has an RMSE of 1.6 ppm, and a band that contains 100%.
  • Quadratic regression with a season has 2.0 ppm. Its band has a nearly constant width of about 3.2 ppm and contains 52%: least squares believes that its residuals are independent, and shows no growing doubt.

It looks like a triumph for version B. But 238 months in a row are not 238 tests: if the forecast is right in 2015 it is likely to be right in 2016. It is closer to one test.

Was that luck? Six starting dates

So we repeat it. Stop the clock at six different dates, learn the kernel from the months before, and forecast the next 15 years:

Code 
origins <- c(1980, 1985, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2007)
rolling <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(origins, function(o) {
    early <- subset(co2, year < o)
    late <- subset(co2, year >= o & year < o + 15)
    if (o == 2007) {
      a <- th_A
      b <- th_B
    } else {
      a <- as.list(exp(
        optim(
          start_A,
          neg_ml,
          t = early$t,
          y = early$ppm - mean(early$ppm),
          parts = parts_A,
          method = "BFGS",
          control = list(maxit = 80)
        )$par
      ))
      b <- as.list(exp(
        optim(
          start_B,
          neg_ml,
          t = early$t,
          y = early$ppm,
          parts = parts_B,
          H = H(early$t),
          method = "BFGS",
          control = list(maxit = 80)
        )$par
      ))
    }
    gA <- gp(early$t, early$ppm - mean(early$ppm), a, parts_A, new = late$t)
    gA$mean <- gA$mean + mean(early$ppm)
    gB <- gp(early$t, early$ppm, b, parts_B, H(early$t), late$t, H(late$t))
    q <- predict(update(quad, data = early), late, interval = "prediction")
    cov <- function(m, s) mean(abs(m - late$ppm) < 1.96 * s)
    data.frame(
      start = o,
      trend_scale_A = a$l1,
      rmse_A = rmse(gA$mean, late$ppm),
      rmse_B = rmse(gB$mean, late$ppm),
      rmse_lm = rmse(q[, 1], late$ppm),
      cover_A = cov(gA$mean, gA$sd),
      cover_B = cov(gB$mean, gB$sd),
      cover_lm = mean(late$ppm > q[, 2] & late$ppm < q[, 3])
    )
  })
)
print(round(rolling, 2), row.names = FALSE)
 start trend_scale_A rmse_A rmse_B rmse_lm cover_A cover_B cover_lm
  1980         36.41   1.76   1.59    1.64    0.99    0.84     0.72
  1985         42.52   2.37   4.06    4.10    0.88    0.33     0.28
  1990         51.27   2.70   5.15    5.36    0.45    0.06     0.06
  1995         24.02  12.12   0.63    2.37    0.12    1.00     0.14
  2000         51.49   5.20   0.45    0.66    0.36    0.99     1.00
  2007         77.44   4.08   1.11    1.42    0.61    1.00     0.68

The triumph is gone:

  • B is excellent from 1995 on (RMSE between 0.5 and 1.1 ppm). Started in 1985 or 1990 it is 4.1 and 5.2 ppm off, and its 95% bands contain 33% and 6% of the months. The quadratic learned from a rise that was speeding up quickly, and in the early 1990s the rise slowed down for some years.
  • A is better in those two cases (2.4 and 2.7 ppm). But after the slowdown it has learned a short length scale for the trend (24.0 years from the data until 1994, 51.3 from the data until 1989) and runs back to the mean at once: 12.1 ppm off.
  • No model has a 95% band with about 95% coverage at all six dates. The coverage goes from 6% to 100% for B and from 12% to 99% for A.

So what are the error bars of a GP worth? Inside the data they are honest. Outside they are honest only if the kernel and the mean function are right, and the data of the past cannot prove that: in section 4 the leave-one-out errors of the two versions were the same. The bands count the functions that the model considers possible. A future that the model forbids is not counted, however wide the band.

6. Taking the curve apart

The sum of kernels can be taken apart again: the posterior mean of each part is its own kernel, multiplied by the same weights. Here with the whole record:

Code 
K <- kernel(co2$t, co2$t, th_B, parts_B); diag(K) <- diag(K) + th_B$sigma^2
beta_all <- solve(crossprod(H(co2$t), solve(K, H(co2$t))), crossprod(H(co2$t), solve(K, co2$ppm)))
weights_all <- solve(K, co2$ppm - H(co2$t) %*% beta_all)
comp <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = co2$year, v = drop(H(co2$t) %*% beta_all), part = "quadratic mean"),
  data.frame(
    year = co2$year,
    v = drop(part(co2$t, co2$t, th_B, "season") %*% weights_all),
    part = "season"
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = co2$year,
    v = drop(part(co2$t, co2$t, th_B, "swings") %*% weights_all),
    part = "swings"
  )
)
comp$part <- factor(comp$part, levels = unique(comp$part))
ggplot(comp, aes(year, v)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~part, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "The three parts of the fitted function", x = NULL, y = "ppm") +
  theme_bw()
Code 
swing <- subset(comp, part == "swings")
amp <- tapply(subset(comp, part == "season")$v, floor(co2$year), function(v) diff(range(v)))
cbind(
  value = c(
    amplitude_of_the_season_1960 = amp[["1960"]],
    amplitude_2020 = amp[["2020"]],
    largest_swing = swing$v[which.max(abs(swing$v))],
    in_year = swing$year[which.max(abs(swing$v))]
  )
)
                                   value
amplitude_of_the_season_1960    5.758639
amplitude_2020                  6.692789
largest_swing                   2.294849
in_year                      1988.791700
  • The seasonal wave grew from 5.8 ppm in 1960 to 6.7 in 2020 (from the lowest to the highest month). Fixed sine waves cannot show that.
  • The swings reach 2.3 ppm, in 1988, and then fall back within a few years. That is the slowdown which threw both forecasts of section 5 off the track.

7. Things to keep in mind

  • The kernel is the model. Length scales are what you report and defend. Try others (Matérn instead of the squared exponential, which is often too smooth).
  • The mean function matters little inside the data and a great deal outside. Test forecasts from several starting dates, not one.
  • Standardise the predictors; with several, give each its own length scale (automatic relevance determination).
  • The cost grows with \(n^3\). A few thousand rows are comfortable; beyond that use approximations (inducing points, nearest neighbours, state space).
  • The marginal likelihood can have several maxima. Start from several points. With few data the length scale may run to an absurd value: put a prior on it.
  • Plugging in the estimates of the kernel’s parameters ignores their uncertainty, and the bands are a bit too narrow. Full Bayesian versions average over them.
  • Other names: kriging in geostatistics, smoothing splines (a GP with a special kernel), Bayesian linear regression (a GP with a linear kernel), support vector regression with the same kernel but without probabilities.
  • Not normal outcomes (counts, yes or no) need approximations: mgcv with bs = "gp", brms with gp().

8. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the mean function, the kernel with its parameters in understandable units, how they were estimated, the accuracy on unseen data, and the coverage of the intervals. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model = rownames(scores),
  rmse = f2(scores[, "RMSE"]),
  cov = pct(scores[, "coverage_95"]),
  width = f1(scores[, "mean_width"])
)

Method (data analysis):

Monthly mean CO₂ concentrations at Mauna Loa from 1958 to 2006 (N = 586; Lan & Keeling, 2026) were modelled with Gaussian process regression (Rasmussen & Williams, 2006). The mean function was quadratic in time with unknown coefficients; the covariance function was the sum of a periodic kernel with a slowly changing shape (period one year), an exponential kernel, and noise. The parameters of the kernel were estimated by maximising the marginal likelihood. A model with a constant mean and an additional squared exponential kernel, and a quadratic regression with seasonal terms, served for comparison. The models were evaluated by leave-one-out prediction of the months until 2006, on the 238 months since 2007, and on 15-year forecasts from six starting dates between 1980 and 2007 (parameters re-estimated each time), with the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the coverage of 95% prediction intervals. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

The Gaussian process with a quadratic mean predicted the months since 2007 with an RMSE of 1.58 ppm, and its 95% intervals contained 100% of the measurements (Table 1). With a constant mean the RMSE was 6.09 ppm and the coverage 46%. In leave-one-out prediction of the months until 2006 the two models had the same RMSE (0.24 ppm) and a coverage of 95%. The advantage of the quadratic mean was not stable: in 15-year forecasts from six starting dates its RMSE ranged from 0.5 to 5.2 ppm and its coverage from 6% to 100%; with a constant mean the ranges were 1.8 to 12.1 ppm and 12% to 99%. In the model of the full record the seasonal amplitude was 5.8 ppm in 1960 and 6.7 ppm in 2020. The estimated length scales were 156 years for the shape of the season and 3.3 years for the irregular swings.

Table 1

Forecasts of Monthly CO₂ Since 2007 From the Record Until 2006

Model RMSE (ppm) Coverage of 95% intervals Mean width (ppm)
A: zero-mean GP 6.09 46% 8.9
B: GP with a quadratic mean 1.58 100% 5.9
quadratic regression + season (lm) 1.97 52% 3.2

Note. 238 months.

Points to remember:

  • State the mean function and the kernel, and what each part stands for.
  • Give length scales in the units of the predictor.
  • Check coverage, not only accuracy, and say whether it was inside or outside the data.
  • Mark forecasts beyond the data as depending on the mean function and the kernel.

9. Summary

When Smooth unknown functions, up to a few thousand rows, and a need for uncertainty
The model \(f \sim \text{GP}(m, k)\); \(y = f + \varepsilon\)
Prediction \(k_*^\top(K + \sigma^2I)^{-1}y\), with variance \(k_{**} - k_*^\top(K + \sigma^2I)^{-1}k_*\)
Kernel parameters Maximum of the marginal likelihood
Building Add kernels for trend, season, swings; take the fit apart again
How (R) Two short functions by hand, or kernlab::gausspr(), mgcv::gam(s(x, bs = "gp")), brms::brm(y ~ gp(x))
Check Leave-one-out errors and coverage; forecasts from several starting dates
Danger Extrapolation follows the mean function and the kernel, and the bands believe both
Related pages Polynomial regression, splines and GAMs, support vector regression

References

Lan, X., & Keeling, R. (2026). Monthly mean CO₂ at Mauna Loa Observatory [Data set]. NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory and Scripps Institution of Oceanography. https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/

Rasmussen, C. E., & Williams, C. K. I. (2006). Gaussian processes for machine learning. MIT Press. https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/3206.001.0001

Roberts, S., Osborne, M., Ebden, M., Reece, S., Gibson, N., & Aigrain, S. (2013). Gaussian processes for time-series modelling. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 371(1984), Article 20110550. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2011.0550

item.title: k-Nearest Neighbours Regression: What Is This House Worth? Ask the Neighbours
item.description: k-nearest neighbours regression in R, by hand and with FNN, on 21,600 house sales around Seattle: distances, scaling and weighting the predictors, choosing k by validation on later sales, the bias-variance trade-off, comparable houses for one sale, the curse of dimensionality with noise predictors, kNN against regression, GAM and random forest, a local correction of a regression, prediction intervals by conformal prediction, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
k-nearest neighbours regression in R, by hand and with FNN, on 21,600 house sales around Seattle: distances, scaling and weighting the predictors, choosing k by validation on later sales, the bias-variance trade-off, comparable houses for one sale, the curse of dimensionality with noise predictors, kNN against regression, GAM and random forest, a local correction of a regression, prediction intervals by conformal prediction, and APA reporting.

The question: what an estate agent does

How do you find out what a house is worth? You look at what similar houses nearby were sold for, and take something like the average. Estate agents call these houses comparables. No formula, no coefficients.

k-nearest neighbours (kNN) is this, done by a computer. To predict a case, find the \(k\) most similar cases in the data and average their outcomes. It is the simplest method of machine learning, more than 70 years old (Fix and Hodges described it in 1951; Cover & Hart, 1967, worked out how good it can be), and it has no training at all. The whole model is the data.

All the difficulty is in two words: how many (k), and what is similar. Is a house of the same size at a distance of 3 km more similar than a house twice as large next door?

Code 
library(FNN)        # knn.reg(), get.knnx(): fast neighbours
library(mgcv)       # bam(), for comparison (comes with R)
library(ranger)     # random forest, for comparison
library(ggplot2)
# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

1. The data

The county around Seattle (King County, Washington) publishes every sale of a house. This file has the sales from May 2014 to May 2015, and OpenML (2019) serves it as CSV:

Code 
raw <- read.csv("https://www.openml.org/data/get_csv/21578898/house_sales.arff")
house <- with(
  raw,
  data.frame(
    price = price,
    logp = log10(price),
    date = as.Date(substr(date, 1, 8), "%Y%m%d"),
    east = (long + 122.2) * 111.32 * cos(47.56 * pi / 180),
    north = (lat - 47.56) * 111.32, # kilometres from a point in the middle
    lsize = log2(sqft_living),
    grade,
    built = yr_built,
    llot = log2(sqft_lot),
    view,
    water = as.integer(waterfront),
    zip = factor(zipcode)
  )
)
nrow(house)
[1] 21613
Code 
range(house$date)
[1] "2014-05-02" "2015-05-27"
Code 
quantile(house$price, c(0.01, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99))
       1%       25%       50%       75%       99% 
 153500.4  321950.0  450000.0  645000.0 1964400.0

There are 21,613 sales. east and north are the position in kilometres, lsize the living space (log base 2, so one unit is a doubling), grade the county’s grade of the building (1 to 13), built the year, llot the land (log), view (0 to 4) and water (on the waterfront). Prices are skewed, so we predict \(\log_{10}\) of the price; an error of 0.04 is about 10%.

The use of such a model is to value houses that are sold later. So we learn from the sales until January 2015, choose the settings with those of February and March, and test with April and May:

Code 
train <- subset(house, date < as.Date("2015-02-01"))
valid <- subset(house, date >= as.Date("2015-02-01") & date < as.Date("2015-04-01"))
test  <- subset(house, date >= as.Date("2015-04-01"))
c(train = nrow(train), validation = nrow(valid), test = nrow(test))
     train validation       test 
     15611       3125       2877

2. Look at the data

Code 
ggplot(train, aes(east, north, colour = logp)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    name = "price",
    breaks = log10(c(1e5, 2.5e5, 5e5, 1e6, 2.5e6)),
    labels = c("100k", "250k", "500k", "1M", "2.5M"),
    limits = log10(c(1.5e5, 2.5e6)),
    oob = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(title = "House prices around Seattle", x = "km east", y = "km north") +
  theme_bw()

Place matters, and not in a way that a straight line could follow: there are expensive shores, cheap corridors and sharp borders.

3. The method step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a distance

The usual one is Euclidean. With the predictors \(x_1, \dots, x_p\),

\[d(x, x') = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2\, (x_j - x'_j)^2}\]

The weights \(w_j\) are part of the method, whether one chooses them or not. If a predictor is measured in other units, its weight changes.

Step 2: the neighbours, and their mean

Let \(N_k(x)\) be the \(k\) training cases with the smallest distance to \(x\). The prediction is

\[\hat f(x) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in N_k(x)} y_i\]

By hand, for the first house of the validation set, with place and size only:

Code 
new <- valid[1, ]
d <- sqrt(
  (train$east - new$east)^2 + (train$north - new$north)^2 + (2 * (train$lsize - new$lsize))^2
) # a doubling of the size counts as 2 km
near <- order(d)[1:5]
cbind(
  distance = round(d[near], 2),
  km = round(sqrt((train$east[near] - new$east)^2 + (train$north[near] - new$north)^2), 2),
  train[near, c("price", "built", "grade")],
  size = round(2^train$lsize[near])
)
      distance   km  price built grade size
16518     0.90 0.78 304000  1972     7  900
6006      0.94 0.67 300000  1982     7  970
16644     0.97 0.31 335000  1967     7 1060
6767      1.03 0.67 350000  1967     7 1010
17242     1.04 0.93 300000  1971     7  910
Code 
c(predicted = 10^mean(train$logp[near]), sold_for = new$price)
predicted  sold_for 
 317136.2  180000.0

Step 3: the choice of \(k\)

With \(k = 1\) the prediction jumps from house to house and copies every accident of a single sale: no bias, much variance. With \(k = n\) it is the mean of all houses: no variance, much bias. In between is the best value, and it must be found by trying.

Step 4: no training, slow prediction

There is nothing to estimate. But for each new case all the distances must be computed. Programs use search trees (FNN does) that avoid most of the work in few dimensions.

4. What is similar? Scaling

Try three definitions, each with several \(k\), on the validation sales:

Code 
vars <- c("east", "north", "lsize", "grade", "built", "llot", "view", "water")
centre <- colMeans(train[, vars]); spread <- apply(train[, vars], 2, sd)
Z <- function(d, w = rep(1, length(vars))) {
  sweep(sweep(sweep(as.matrix(d[, vars]), 2, centre), 2, spread, "/"), 2, w, "*")
} # standardise with the training data, then weight
knn <- function(Ztr, Zte, k, y = train$logp) knn.reg(Ztr, Zte, y, k = k)$pred
ks <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 35, 60, 100)
place <- c("east", "north")
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    k = ks,
    rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) rmse(knn(train[, place], valid[, place], k), valid$logp)),
    what = "place only"
  ),
  data.frame(
    k = ks,
    rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) rmse(knn(train[, vars], valid[, vars], k), valid$logp)),
    what = "all predictors, raw units"
  ),
  data.frame(
    k = ks,
    rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) rmse(knn(Z(train), Z(valid), k), valid$logp)),
    what = "all predictors, standardised"
  )
)
best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(curves, curves$what), function(d) d[which.min(d$rmse), ]))
best
                              k       rmse                         what
all predictors, raw units     5 0.10989469    all predictors, raw units
all predictors, standardised 12 0.09012174 all predictors, standardised
place only                    8 0.12973096                   place only
Code 
ggplot(curves, aes(k, rmse, colour = what)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = ks) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eda100", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Error on later sales, by the number of neighbours",
    x = "k (log scale)",
    y = "RMSE of log10(price)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  • The classic U-shape: too few neighbours are noisy, too many are not similar.
  • With place only, 0.130 at best.
  • With all the predictors in raw units, 0.110. The year of construction runs over a hundred units and the waterfront over one, so the years decide who is a neighbour.
  • Standardised, 0.090. Each predictor has the same weight now.

Weights for the predictors

But why the same weight? Place matters more than the size of the garden. We can search for better weights on the validation set, one predictor at a time, doubling or halving its weight as long as it helps:

Code 
w <- setNames(rep(1, length(vars)), vars)
score <- function(w, k = 8) rmse(knn(Z(train, w), Z(valid, w), k), valid$logp)
current <- score(w); history <- data.frame(step = 0, changed = "start", rmse = current)
for (round in 1:4) {
  for (v in vars) {
    for (f in c(2, 0.5)) {
      repeat {
        trial <- w
        trial[v] <- trial[v] * f
        s <- score(trial)
        if (s < current - 1e-5) {
          w <- trial
          current <- s
          history <- rbind(history, data.frame(step = nrow(history), changed = v, rmse = s))
        } else {
          break
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
w
 east north lsize grade built  llot  view water 
 8.00  4.00  2.00  1.00  0.25  1.00  0.25  1.00
Code 
k_w <- ks[which.min(sapply(ks, function(k) score(w, k)))]
c(standardised = best["all predictors, standardised", "rmse"], weighted = score(w, k_w), k = k_w)
standardised     weighted            k 
  0.09012174   0.08359334   8.00000000

The search gives the most weight to east, north, lsize, and the error falls to 0.084. The weights are the model. They were tuned on the validation sales, so that error is too good; the test set will tell. (Weighting the neighbours themselves by their distance is another refinement, which helps a little.)

5. The comparables of one house

An advantage that few other methods of machine learning have: the prediction can be shown.

Code 
Zt <- Z(train, w); Zn <- Z(test, w)
one <- 3
nn <- get.knnx(Zt, Zn[one, , drop = FALSE], k = k_w)
comp <- train[nn$nn.index[1, ], ]
show <- rbind(
  cbind(what = "to be valued", test[one, ]),
  cbind(what = paste("neighbour", seq_len(k_w)), comp)
)
data.frame(
  what = show$what,
  price = f0(show$price),
  sqft = round(2^show$lsize),
  grade = show$grade,
  built = show$built,
  km = round(sqrt((show$east - test$east[one])^2 + (show$north - test$north[one])^2), 1),
  row.names = NULL
)
